Is it perfect? No. The romance is underdeveloped and the least interesting part of the book, though it presents some changes to the usual formula, and some situations are solved a bit too easily, but nothing that would lower my rating. I don't have many complaints.

I'm excited to see what Vanessa Len brings next and to see what happens in the next book.
description:
With the sweeping romance of Passenger and the dark fantasy edge of This Savage Song, this standout YA contemporary fantasy debut from Vanessa Len, is the first in a planned trilogy.

It should have been the perfect summer. Sent to stay with her late mother’s eccentric family in London, sixteen-year-old Joan is determined to enjoy herself. She loves her nerdy job at the historic Holland House, and when her super cute co-worker Nick asks her on a date, it feels like everything is falling into place.

But she soon learns the truth. Her family aren’t just eccentric: they’re monsters, with terrifying, hidden powers. And Nick isn’t just a cute boy: he’s a legendary monster slayer, who will do anything to bring them down.

As she battles Nick, Joan is forced to work with the beautiful and ruthless Aaron Oliver, heir to a monster family that hates her own. She’ll have to embrace her own monstrousness if she is to save herself, and her family. Because in this story . . .

. . . she is not the hero.

title: Abaddon’s Gate (The Expanse, #3)
author: James S.A. Corey
review: It does have a slow start and it takes some time to get used to the new characters, but I still had an amazing time with this book, and I just wished more people looked beyond the ugly covers so they could discover the fabulous world and characters that The Expanse has.
description:
Abaddon's Gate is the third book in the New York Times bestselling Expanse series.

For generations, the solar system - Mars, the Moon, the Asteroid Belt - was humanity's great frontier. Until now. The alien artefact working through its program under the clouds of Venus has emerged to build a massive structure outside the orbit of Uranus: a gate that leads into a starless dark.

Jim Holden and the crew of the Rocinante are part of a vast flotilla of scientific and military ships going out to examine the artefact. But behind the scenes, a complex plot is unfolding, with the destruction of Holden at its core. As the emissaries of the human race try to find whether the gate is an opportunity or a threat, the greatest danger is the one they brought with them.

title: Caliban's War (The Expanse, #2)
author: James S.A. Corey
review:
I'm a little behind in posting this review, but I'll keep it short because it's the second book in a sci-fi series (that no one seems to read btw) that, while enjoyable, repeats the same beats from the first one.

Of course, the problem has evolved, and the actions and consequences are different this time around, but the general feeling that comes from the "adventure" part of the story is just like in 'Leviathan Wakes.' I'm not criticizing, though. If something's not broken, don't fix it, and I think the formula in this series can hold well enough for a few more books without getting tiresome.

But let's be realistic: the main reason why I love this series is the characters. I've rarely encountered a better set of characters in a book, let alone a book series. Every single one had something to do, and you're rooting for them to succeed.

Yes, the villains are caricatures, and their plans are thought out poorly, but it's part of the charm. I feel like they come from the Looney Tunes ACME villains where they are just evil with no reason and not even they are sure of what to do, but it's fun.

I don't have much to add. I liked it. I'll be reading the next one (especially after that cliffhanger), and I hope more people discover these books. I'm sure that if the same plot were used in a fantasy setting, this would have been a hit on Booktok and Bookstagram.
description:
Итак, мы не одиноки.
На Ганимеде, житнице внешних планет, марсианка-спецназовец становится свидетелем гибели своего взвода, истребленного чудовищным суперсолдатом. На Земле высокопоставленный политик изо всех сил пытается предотвратить межпланетную войну.
А на Венере обосновалась чуждая протомолекула, производя таинственные трансформации и угрожая распространиться по Солнечной системе.
В бескрайнем космосе Джеймс Холден и экипаж "Росинанта" заняты поддержанием мира от имени Альянса Внешних Планет. Они соглашаются помочь в поисках пропавшего на Ганимеде ребенка и внезапно обнаруживают, что будущее человечества зависит от того, сможет ли один корабль предотвратить межпланетное вторжение, которое, возможно, уже началось...
"Война Калибана" - это твердая научная фантастика, полная головокружительных приключений. Один из лучших образцов жанра последнего времени наряду с "Пробуждением Левиафана".

title: NOS4A2
author: Joe  Hill
description:
Victoria McQueen has a secret gift for finding things: a misplaced bracelet, a missing photograph, answers to unanswerable questions. On her Raleigh Tuff Burner bike, she makes her way to a rickety covered bridge that, within moments, takes her wherever she needs to go, whether it’s across Massachusetts or across the country.

Charles Talent Manx has a way with children. He likes to take them for rides in his 1938 Rolls-Royce Wraith with the NOS4A2 vanity plate. With his old car, he can slip right out of the everyday world, and onto the hidden roads that transport them to an astonishing – and terrifying – playground of amusements he calls “Christmasland.”

Then, one day, Vic goes looking for trouble—and finds Manx. That was a lifetime ago. Now Vic, the only kid to ever escape Manx’s unmitigated evil, is all grown up and desperate to forget. But Charlie Manx never stopped thinking about Victoria McQueen. He’s on the road again and he’s picked up a new passenger: Vic’s own son.

title: The Girl Who Fell Beneath the Sea
author: Axie Oh
review:
A charming, cute, little book.

I had a good time but it’s nothing earth-shattering either. A solid 3.5 star read because I did enjoyed the author’s writing style so I think her future books will be amazing!

The cover is gorgeous tho
description:
Axie Oh's The Girl Who Fell Beneath the Sea is an enthralling retelling of a classic Korean folktale, perfect for fans of Wintersong, Uprooted, and Miyazaki’s Spirited Away.

Deadly storms have ravaged Mina’s homeland for generations. Floods sweep away entire villages, while bloody wars are waged over the few remaining resources. Her people believe the Sea God, once their protector, now curses them with death and despair. In an attempt to appease him, each year a beautiful maiden is thrown into the sea to serve as the Sea God’s bride, in the hopes that one day the “true bride” will be chosen and end the suffering.

Many believe that Shim Cheong, the most beautiful girl in the village—and the beloved of Mina’s older brother Joon—may be the legendary true bride. But on the night Cheong is to be sacrificed, Joon follows Cheong out to sea, even knowing that to interfere is a death sentence. To save her brother, Mina throws herself into the water in Cheong’s stead.

Swept away to the Spirit Realm, a magical city of lesser gods and mythical beasts, Mina seeks out the Sea God, only to find him caught in an enchanted sleep. With the help of a mysterious young man named Shin—as well as a motley crew of demons, gods and spirits—Mina sets out to wake the Sea God and bring an end to the killer storms once and for all.

But she doesn’t have much time: A human cannot live long in the land of the spirits. And there are those who would do anything to keep the Sea God from waking…

title: Foul Lady Fortune (Foul Lady Fortune, #1)
author: Chloe Gong
review:
It does have some great twists during the second half, but a slow start and so-so main characters bring down the enjoyment of the book, overall.

Of course I’m still going to read every single Chloe Gong book.
description:
It’s 1931 in Shanghai, and the stage is set for a new decade of intrigue.

Four years ago, Rosalind Lang was brought back from the brink of death, but the strange experiment that saved her also stopped her from sleeping and aging—and allows her to heal from any wound. In short, Rosalind cannot die. Now, desperate for redemption for her traitorous past, she uses her abilities as an assassin for her country.

Code name: Fortune.

But when the Japanese Imperial Army begins its invasion march, Rosalind’s mission pivots. A series of murders is causing unrest in Shanghai, and the Japanese are under suspicion. Rosalind’s new orders are to infiltrate foreign society and identify the culprits behind the terror plot before more of her people are killed.

To reduce suspicion, however, she must pose as the wife of another Nationalist spy, Orion Hong, and though Rosalind finds Orion’s cavalier attitude and playboy demeanor infuriating, she is willing to work with him for the greater good. But Orion has an agenda of his own, and Rosalind has secrets that she wants to keep buried. As they both attempt to unravel the conspiracy, the two spies soon find that there are deeper and more horrifying layers to this mystery than they ever imagined.

From the #1 New York Times bestselling author of These Violent Delights and Our Violent Ends comes the first book in a captivating new duology following an ill-matched pair of spies posing as a married couple to investigate a series of brutal murders in 1930s Shanghai.

title: Gods & Monsters (Serpent & Dove, #3)
author: Shelby Mahurin
review:
And just like that, I finished the 'Serpent and Dove' series.

Now, it wasn't my favorite, but it had all the ingredients I needed to keep me entertained, even if it does suffer from an overlong situation, especially in this last book.

And by writing that, I remembered how different my perception of this series is while comparing it to how others received it. While most people LOVED the first one, I just liked it, then while a lot of reviewers slammed the sequel, I enjoyed it greatly, but I think I found some common ground in this third one. Some people loved it, and some people just plainly liked it. I'm on the "just liked it" side.

I'm still rating it with 4-stars because it gives everything a fantasy trilogy ending should have. The characters bring their A game (Beau being a personal fave), and some interesting developments happen, but I just wished that Shelby Mahurin gave the villains a sense of purpose. I mean, does anyone really remember what Morgane wanted? Does anyone care?

She was just evil for the sake of being evil, and that's just boring. Josephine was a bit more interesting and Nicholina is probably the most nuanced villain of all, but with some lame fights at end, it just felt like a "we need to hurry to the end" situation.

All in all, it was a good series. It wouldn't be the first one I recommend, but it was solid.
description:
Evil always seeks a foothold. We must not give it one. The electrifying conclusion to the New York Times and Indiebound bestselling Serpent & Dove series is perfect for fans of Sarah J. Maas and Kendare Blake.

Lou has spent her whole life running. Now, after a crushing blow from Morgane, the time has come to go home—and claim what is rightfully hers.

But this is no longer the Lou her friends knew. No longer the Lou who captured a chasseur’s heart. A darkness has settled over her, and this time it will take more than love to drive it out.

title: Red Rising (Red Rising, #1)
author: Pierce Brown
description:
The Earth is dying.

Darrow is a Red, a miner in the interior of Mars. His mission is to extract enough precious elements to one day tame the surface of the planet and allow humans to live on it.
The Reds are humanity's last hope.

Or so it appears, until the day Darrow discovers it's all a lie.

That Mars has been habitable - and inhabited - for generations, by a class of people calling themselves the Golds.

A class of people who look down on Darrow and his fellows as slave labour, to be exploited and worked to death without a second thought. Until the day that Darrow, with the help of a mysterious group of rebels, disguises himself as a Gold and infiltrates their command school, intent on taking down his oppressors from the inside.

But the command school is a battlefield - and Darrow isn't the only student with an agenda.

Break the chains.

Live for more.

This edition contains a preview of Golden Son, Book II of the Red Rising trilogy.

title: The Final Gambit (The Inheritance Games, #3)
author: Jennifer Lynn Barnes
review:
Oh, the disappointment…

Did we really need a new Big Bad in the last book of a series? And even worse, in the last half?

It’s awful when those things happen, yet here we are!

I didn’t hate this one, but the previous books promised a BIG ending, and it was mostly a bummer: obvious and unfulfilling plot twists, a convoluted mystery, a boring villain and an anti-climactic final match.

Also, I don’t know if this just happens in this particular book or it happened since the first one and I never noticed it, but the author is committed to using the full name of the characters not just when she introduces a character, but even randomly in the dialogue and in Avery’s narration. I’m not sure why, but it irked me. Once or twice was fine, but it happened constantly and it just became annoying and silly really quick.

Oh well, at least the journey was mostly fun and the covers are to die for.
description:
Avery’s fortune, life, and loves are on the line in the game that everyone will be talking about.

To inherit billions, all Avery Kylie Grambs has to do is survive a few more weeks living in Hawthorne House. The paparazzi are dogging her every step. Financial pressures are building. Danger is a fact of life. And the only thing getting Avery through it all is the Hawthorne brothers. Her life is intertwined with theirs. She knows their secrets and they know her.

But as the clock ticks down to the moment when Avery will become the richest teenager on the planet, trouble arrives in the form of a visitor who needs her help—and whose presence in Hawthorne House could change everything. It soon becomes clear that there is one last puzzle to solve, and Avery and the Hawthorne brothers are drawn into a dangerous game against an unknown and powerful player.

title: Kingdom of the Cursed (Kingdom of the Wicked, #2)
author: Kerri Maniscalco
review:
Well... that was something.

I don't think I ever had a guilty pleasure when it came to books before, but now I think I definitely have one, and this series is the one.

'Kingdom of the Cursed' is something that I can't really explain. Is it good? Not really, there is not much sense of a plot in here, but mostly a compilation of random scenes with different characters and scenarios that seem to have the final purpose of solving the mystery (?) that the first book introduced in a mostly satisfactory fashion. However, this one doesn't seem to care much about that, and especially during its first half, is more interested in reminding us that our main girl Emilia is filled with lusty thoughts about our favorite evil entity Wrath.

Now, I don't really mind steamy scenes in books. I know my genre and most of these YA/NA series are filled with these, but I was astonished by the creativeness that Kerri Maniscalco needed to have to be able to transform EVERY single thought Emilia could have, in a monologue of why she couldn't possibly ever love Wrath, but at the same time remind us how horny she was for him. And that's the main adjective for this book: it is horny. It's not even the most NSFW book out there, but I've never encountered so many horny characters in a single book and it was an experience just because of that.

And it was the reason why I wasn't feeling the book during the first 70 pages or so. In the previous one, Maniscalco was running towards a mystery endgame, where there was a puzzle mostly grounded on a whodunit scenario. On this one, every notion of that was thrown out of the window and instead it became more of a romance with a semblance of a plot sprinkled on top, but c'mon... Kerri just wanted to get to the next sex scene. And one as a reader did too, because the mystery doesn't seem important anymore.

And that's probably because not even the characters care that much about the murders that were so important in the last book. Yeah, sometimes they were mentioned and Emilia got mad because of the lack of any progression regarding to them, but nothing that a "wicked grin" from Wrath couldn't help with.

Also, am I the only one that noticed how we didn't get a SINGLE answer in more than 400 pages? Yes, we do get a big reveal at the end, but other than that, every question Emilia, and therefore we as readers could have, fall into this vague sort of answer where only the hooded-and-mysterious-character knows what it means, because we still have a book left, so we need to remain in the dark.

Oh well... now that I think about it, it may seem like I didn't liked it, but that's not true. I had a good time with it. I like the characters and I sort of appreciate how silly and unnecessarily contrived the story really is, so I'll be reading the next one but oh my... how covers are deceiving.
description:
After selling her soul to become Queen of the Wicked, Emilia travels to the Seven Circles with the enigmatic Prince of Wrath, where she’s introduced to a seductive world of vice.

She vows to do whatever it takes to avenge her beloved sister, Vittoria... even if that means accepting the hand of the Prince of Pride, the king of demons.

The first rule in the court of the Wicked? Trust no one. With back-stabbing princes, luxurious palaces, mysterious party invitations, and conflicting clues about who really killed her twin, Emilia finds herself more alone than ever before. Can she even trust Wrath, her one-time ally in the mortal world... or is he keeping dangerous secrets about his true nature?

Emilia will be tested in every way as she seeks a series of magical objects that will unlock the clues of her past and the answers she craves...

One sister.
Two sinful princes.
Infinite deception with a side of revenge… Welcome to Hell.

From #1 New York Times bestselling author of Stalking Jack the Ripper Kerri Maniscalco comes the sizzling, sweepingly romantic sequel to Kingdom of the Wicked!

title: A Gentleman in Moscow
author: Amor Towles
review:
Well, this was way out of my confort zone, and that was good.

Admittedly, even though now I'm more of a fantasy reader, I used to be a contemporary/thriller/historical fiction kind of guy, but even THEN, this book would have never caught my attention just by reading the synopsis. It was actually recommended to me so that's why I decided to read it, and it was an experience.

It doesn't really have a *plot* in the common way and it's more of a mix of several subplots that follow our main character during his house arrest in a luxurious hotel, so that way you get to know a handful of characters that populate the hotel and their connection with the Count. Since the book spans decades, all these subplots are presented in an on and off kind of way which helps to keep it interesting and dynamic, even though, like I said, there's no main plot line.

I think actually, that the most interesting thing about the book it's how it is written. Amor Towles writes in a fun, kind of philosophical but approachable way that doesn't make the book feel tiring or heavy. In fact, I was surprised by how addicting it is considering that it's more of a character driven slow book. Which may also be its downfall for some.

The book IS slow. There's no action or suspense, and I think that this might turn someone off at first, and then when you really got the hang of it, on the last 50 pages it becomes kind of an espionage thing that wasn't really my cup of tea but I accepted it and moved on.

In summary, I liked it. Will it become a personal fave? I don't think so, but would I recommend it? Not to everyone, I think it appeals to more of a niche audience, but to the right person, I think I would.
description:
He can't leave. You won't want to.

With his breakout novel Rules of Civility, Amor Towles established himself as a master of absorbing, sophisticated fiction, bringing late-1930s Manhattan to life with splendid atmosphere and a flawless command of style. A Gentleman in Moscow immerses us in another elegantly drawn era with the story of Count Alexander Rostov.

When, in 1922, the thirty-year-old Count is deemed an unrepentant aristocrat by a Bolshevik tribunal, he is sentenced to house arrest in the Metropol, a grand hotel across the street from the Kremlin. An indomitable man of erudition and wit, Rostov must now live in an attic room while some of the most tumultuous decades in Russian history are unfolding outside the hotel’s doors.

Unexpectedly, the Count's reduced circumstances provide him entry to a much larger world of emotional discovery as he forges friendships with the hotel's other denizens, including a willful actress, a shrewd Kremlinite, a gregarious American, and a temperamental chef. But when fate suddenly puts the life of a young girl in his hands, he must draw on all his ingenuity to protect the future she so deserves.

Brimming with humor, a glittering cast of characters, and one beautifully rendered scene after another, this singular novel casts a spell as it relates the Count’s endeavor to gain a deeper understanding of what it means to be a man of purpose.

title: Rock Paper Scissors
author: Alice Feeney
description:
Think you know the person you married? Think again…

Things have been wrong with Mr and Mrs Wright for a long time. When Adam and Amelia win a weekend away to Scotland, it might be just what their marriage needs. Self-confessed workaholic and screenwriter Adam Wright has lived with face blindness his whole life. He can’t recognize friends or family, or even his own wife.

Every anniversary the couple exchange traditional gifts – paper, cotton, pottery, tin – and each year Adam’s wife writes him a letter that she never lets him read. Until now. They both know this weekend will make or break their marriage, but they didn’t randomly win this trip. One of them is lying, and someone doesn’t want them to live happily ever after.

Ten years of marriage. Ten years of secrets. And an anniversary they will never forget.

Rock Paper Scissors is the latest exciting domestic thriller from the queen of the killer twist, New York Times bestselling author Alice Feeney.

title: Namesake (The World of the Narrows, #2)
author: Adrienne Young
review:
Ok, this is one of those times when the Goodreads rating system really puts me in an uncomfortable position.

And that’s because I feel guilty about rating ‘Namesake’ with 3 stars when it’s actually a 3.5, but I just can’t tick it up to 4. It’s not a 4 star read.

For the most part, this book is a more than decent sequel to ‘Fable’, which even if it wasn’t like my favorite book or anything, it was a slightly above average YA adventure with some interesting ideas but not an amazing execution. It lacked stakes, real consequences to the characters actions, it didn’t really fleshed out most of these characters and it had some confusing writing.

Well, ‘Namesake’ doesn’t really care about fixing none of these issues, except for the last one. Now that you’re in this world, everything makes sense to the reader so now you don’t get to feel lost like in the first one. That was nice, but I can’t understand how a pirate story can be so predictable and easy to figure out.

C’mon, I wanted to feel the danger in which Fable was supposedly in during the whole book, but that tension was nowhere to be found. And that only made the whole book fall apart, since because of this, now West felt like an insufferable kid who is being mean to everyone, and Fable like a naive girl who fell into every possible trap the villains laid for her. And the justification for everything was that they were desperate because of the situation they were in, but the situation felt so simple that it never clicked with me why the characters were so nervous in the first place.

I mean, Holland’s built up during these books was so strong, and her actions were described as so ruthless and dangerous, that when we get to the big finale and her “defeat” happens, everything is just SO EASY that it doesn’t even makes sense. Wasn’t she really dangerous? Wasn’t Holland someone no one wanted to cross paths with? And then all of sudden, in just one minute her entire fleet is gone and she’s just okay with it and even “smiles” in her very last scene?

I don’t know, the happy ending felt unearned for Fable, West and the rest of them, and I don’t like that feeling, because it was mostly a pleasant read. I had a fun time, the romance was cute and the characters had a lot of potential (especially Saint) but everything just stayed so superficial that nothing feels like it was fully explored, and that’s a shame.

All in all, this book (and I think the duology in general) is a 3.5 stars.
description:
Welcome to a world made dangerous by the sea and by those who wish to profit from it. Where a young girl must find her place and her family while trying to survive in a world built for men.

With the Marigold ship free of her father, Fable and the rest of the crew were set to start over. That freedom is short-lived when Fable becomes a pawn in a notorious thug’s scheme. In order to get to her intended destination, she must help him to secure a partnership with Holland, a powerful gem trader who is more than she seems.

As Fable descends deeper into a world of betrayal and deception, she learns that the secrets her mother took to her grave are now putting the people Fable cares about in danger. If Fable is going to save them, then she must risk everything—including the boy she loves and the home she has finally found.

title: Our Violent Ends (These Violent Delights, #2)
author: Chloe Gong
review:
If I was a bit skeptical about the second book in this duology after the cliffhanger from ‘These Violent Delights’, Chloe Gong proved me WRONG.

‘Our Violent Ends’ is not just a great sequel, it’s an even-better-than-the-original sequel in every single way. There is angst aplenty, a heart wrenching romance, an amazing cast of characters (Benedikt being my biggest highlight, besides Juliette, of course) and twists from start to finish.

Maybe the historical background that surrounds the plot isn’t as exciting as other conflicts that have happened in history, but the way it connects to the story is amazing and totally deserved.

And even if I was hoping for a different type of ending, I must applaud the guts that the author had to go all the way through with what happened at the end, especially because you can just feel how much she cared and gave thought to these books, so I’m sure she sometimes regretted what had to be the ultimate ending.

Overall, an amazing duology that I can’t help but recommend. Yes, the first book takes its time to fully start, but once you move past that and discover the great characters and the enormous complexity that really entails behind the situation that Juliette and Roma are living, you won’t regret it.

Something I did wonder about these books is how are they considered YA? It’s far too adult and too complex for this demographic, I think. Yes, the characters are 19 and 18, but that’s where the “teen” part ends.
description:
The year is 1927, and Shanghai teeters on the edge of revolution.

After sacrificing her relationship with Roma to protect him from the blood feud, Juliette has been a girl on a mission. One wrong move, and her cousin will step in to usurp her place as the Scarlet Gang’s heir. The only way to save the boy she loves from the wrath of the Scarlets is to have him want her dead for murdering his best friend in cold blood. If Juliette were actually guilty of the crime Roma believes she committed, his rejection might sting less.

Roma is still reeling from Marshall’s death, and his cousin Benedikt will barely speak to him. Roma knows it’s his fault for letting the ruthless Juliette back into his life, and he’s determined to set things right—even if that means killing the girl he hates and loves with equal measure.

Then a new monstrous danger emerges in the city, and though secrets keep them apart, Juliette must secure Roma’s cooperation if they are to end this threat once and for all. Shanghai is already at a boiling point: The Nationalists are marching in, whispers of civil war brew louder every day, and gangster rule faces complete annihilation. Roma and Juliette must put aside their differences to combat monsters and politics, but they aren’t prepared for the biggest threat of all: protecting their hearts from each other.

Shanghai is under siege in this captivating and searingly romantic sequel to These Violent Delights, which New York Times bestselling author Natasha Ngan calls “deliciously dark.”

title: The Dragon's Promise (Six Crimson Cranes, #2)
author: Elizabeth Lim
review:
I love this duology so so much!

Yes, it may be a bit too long, but the adventure, the characters and the plot are all amazing!
description:
Princess Shiori made a deathbed promise to return the dragon's pearl to its rightful owner, but keeping that promise is more dangerous than she ever imagined.

She must journey to the kingdom of dragons, navigate political intrigue among humans and dragons alike, fend off thieves who covet the pearl for themselves and will go to any lengths to get it, all while cultivating the appearance of a perfect princess to dissuade those who would see her burned at the stake for the magic that runs in her blood.

The pearl itself is no ordinary cargo; it thrums with malevolent power, jumping to Shiori's aid one minute, and betraying her the next—threatening to shatter her family and sever the thread of fate that binds her to her true love. It will take every ounce of strength Shiori can muster to defend the life and the love she's fought so hard to win.

title: As Good As Dead (A Good Girl's Guide to Murder, #3)
author: Holly  Jackson
review: I HATED the ending, these characters deserved so much more, but besides that last 5%, this trilogy is amazing from start to end.
description:
The finale to A Good Girl's Guide to Murder series. By the end of this mystery series, you'll never think of good girls the same way again...

Pip is about to head to college, but she is still haunted by the way her last investigation ended. She’s used to online death threats in the wake of her viral true-crime podcast, but she can’t help noticing an anonymous person who keeps asking her: Who will look for you when you’re the one who disappears?

Soon the threats escalate and Pip realizes that someone is following her in real life. When she starts to find connections between her stalker and a local serial killer caught six years ago, she wonders if maybe the wrong man is behind bars.

Police refuse to act, so Pip has only one choice: find the suspect herself—or be the next victim. As the deadly game plays out, Pip discovers that everything in her small town is coming full circle... and if she doesn’t find the answers, this time she will be the one who disappears...

title: Daughter of the Moon Goddess (The Celestial Kingdom, #1)
author: Sue Lynn Tan
review:
Oh, how I hate to be disappointed, and yet here I am.

On paper, 'Daughter of the Moon Goddess' had everything I love in a book, and, before reading it, I could have sworn that it was going to be a 5-star one. But it just wasn't.

I don't know. Since the first chapter, something was off, and throughout the book, though there were some nice, interesting parts, I simply didn't like it much.

Thinking back on it, it probably was that I don't care at all about the main character, and why? Because she is perfect. She's the greatest warrior, the cleverest strategist, the one everybody loves, and that can get away from anything just by herself. Xyngyin is the definition of a Mary Sue, and that wasn't fun for me. Even though she goes through many trials, battles, and setbacks, the stakes are always low, and the tension is non-existent.

Also, the romance is the most boring thing I've encountered in YA, even if it does bring a nice twist in the last third. Liwei is simply lame, and Wenzhi though a bit more interesting, didn't shine up to me that much either.

As if it wasn't clear enough, this book wasn't for me, really. However, am I going to read the second one? Ugh, probably, I'm a completionist, and since it's just a duology, it's not that big of a commitment, either. We'll see.
description:
A romantic debut epic fantasy inspired by the legend of the Chinese moon goddess, Chang’e, in which a young woman’s quest to free her mother pits her against the most powerful immortal in the realm.

Growing up on the moon, Xingyin is accustomed to solitude, unaware that she is being hidden from the feared Celestial Emperor who exiled her mother for stealing his elixir of immortality. But when Xingyin’s magic flares and her existence is discovered, she is forced to flee her home, leaving her mother behind.

Alone, powerless, and afraid, she makes her way to the Celestial Kingdom, a land of wonder and secrets. Disguising her identity, she seizes an opportunity to learn alongside the emperor’s son, mastering archery and magic, even as passion flames between her and the prince.

To save her mother, Xingyin embarks on a perilous quest, confronting legendary creatures and vicious enemies. But when treachery looms and forbidden magic threatens the kingdom, she must challenge the ruthless Celestial Emperor for her dream—striking a dangerous bargain in which she is torn between losing all she loves or plunging the realm into chaos.

title: House of Sky and Breath (Crescent City, #2)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
Okay, I needed a whole day to calm down, so I could review this one.

FYI: there will be ONE big spoiler in this review, because the book demands it, but besides that one, everything else will be (I think) spoiler-free.

Now, where do I begin? First things first: Sarah J. Maas is one of my favorite authors even with all of her faults, and 'House of Sky and Breath' cemented 'Crescent City' as my second favorite series of her, and if the next one is as good as the first two, it may even surpass 'Throne of Glass'. For me, it was THAT good.

And it's not even because it has the most interesting story I've ever read, but it has some amazing characters, an intriguing and gigantic world, and it all just feel really epic, in a way that ACOTAR could only wish for and TOG just reached on its last book.

I've read some opinions that it's not as good as the first one, but I think I mostly disagree. You see, the first one has a really rough start. I know why it was that way, and probably if I reread now it wouldn't be as hard to keep track of everything, but for a newbie it's just a lot. And I think that's why I felt this sequel so much better. Once we got rid of the necessary world building, the characters, and the world could just be. Don't get me wrong, there are still a lot of things to get to know and keep track of, but I think that for the most part it all just flows so much better this time, even if sometimes you have to suspend your disbelief a bit too much.

And I know, this is a high fantasy novel, of course you have to suspend your disbelief, but even while in-world, it's laughable how many secrets SJM wants us to believe that Danika had. That girl had a busy month before she died, and I get it, it's probably the only way Bryce would get involved in the whole drama the way that she does, but it feels a bit lazy. I really hope that in future installments, SJM doesn't use this plot device as much as it was here.

Now, let's get into THE ENDING. OMG, I yelled. And that's something that almost never happens. I actually can't remember the last time I was shocked by a book.

Here comes the BIGGEST shock in the book (and probably in any SJM book): Bryce gets to Prythian through a portal. And she's not just there, she meets Rhysand, Feyre and all the gang from the ACOTAR series. If that's not something meant to shock, then I don't know what it is. The twist, the buildup, the tension, and the confusion deserves an A+. Especially because I never thought that would happen.

When I watched the video that Sarah made to celebrate its publication, and she said something about the ending, I imagined a lot of things: maybe Hunt or Ruhn were going to die, probably Bryce was going to kill one of them by accident (I even thought that a Tamlin situation was going to happen in here), it even occurred to me that maybe Bryce would die, but nothing prepared me for that.

Yes, Rhysand and Feyre made a cameo at the end of 'Kingdom of Ash', but that was it… just a cameo. In here, they actually meet Bryce, and they will coexist in the next book, so don't lie by telling me that is not exciting. And even if I'm not the biggest fan of the ACOTAR series, I'm dying to know what happens next (and it forces me to catch up quickly).

I've read a lot of theories about this twist: if this crossover will be just like a one-and-done, or if there are going to be repercussions on both series like in the MCU with the Avengers, and even if Erilea (the world from TOG) could make an appearance. Now that would be amazing. To be totally honest, I would love that.

Some people don't like the real-life repercussion it may bring to her books, like the impossibility of keeping the series apart, the fact that you'll need to read every single book to get the whole picture, or the possibility that it all becomes a cash-grab. There is a certain truth in those fears, but let's be honest… once you like an author, you'll always buy their books, so why get upset about it? Just imagine the possibilities…

I trust wholeheartedly in this twist. Sarah J. Maas has been working on this universe for years, and I'm sure she knows what she is doing, even if all just stays as cameos, or it grows into something bigger, I'm sure it'll be a blast.

Coming back to just the book, I don't really want to say much because I wouldn't like if someone else came to me and told me what happened, but it's just excellent. I read almost the second half in just a day and a half, so that's something.
description:
Bryce Quinlan and Hunt Athalar are trying to get back to normal―they may have saved Crescent City, but with so much upheaval in their lives lately, they mostly want a chance to relax. Slow down. Figure out what the future holds.

The Asteri have kept their word so far, leaving Bryce and Hunt alone. But with the rebels chipping away at the Asteri’s power, the threat the rulers pose is growing. As Bryce, Hunt, and their friends get pulled into the rebels’ plans, the choice becomes clear: stay silent while others are oppressed, or fight for what’s right. And they’ve never been very good at staying silent.

In this sexy, action-packed sequel to the #1 bestseller House of Earth and Blood, Sarah J. Maas weaves a captivating story of a world about to explode―and the people who will do anything to save it.

title: The Prison Healer (The Prison Healer, #1)
author: Lynette Noni
review: More slow-paced than I usually like, but I was entertained the whole time, even if I guessed some of the twists!
description:
Seventeen-year-old Kiva Meridan has spent the last ten years fighting for survival in the notorious death prison, Zalindov, working as the prison healer.

When the Rebel Queen is captured, Kiva is charged with keeping the terminally ill woman alive long enough for her to undergo the Trial by Ordeal: a series of elemental challenges against the torments of air, fire, water, and earth, assigned to only the most dangerous of criminals.

Then a coded message from Kiva’s family arrives, containing a single order: “Don’t let her die. We are coming.” Aware that the Trials will kill the sickly queen, Kiva risks her own life to volunteer in her place. If she succeeds, both she and the queen will be granted their freedom.

But no one has ever survived.

With an incurable plague sweeping Zalindov, a mysterious new inmate fighting for Kiva’s heart, and a prison rebellion brewing, Kiva can’t escape the terrible feeling that her trials have only just begun.

From bestselling author Lynette Noni comes a dark, thrilling YA fantasy perfect for fans of Sarah J. Maas, and Sabaa Tahir.

title: My Best Friend's Exorcism
author: Grady Hendrix
review:
A solid 4.5-star horror read that never goes full horror but does bring a creepy atmosphere and chilling situations where you feel uncomfortable while reading.

Also, it is addicting and portrays friendship in an 80's kind of way that works phenomenally. I read in different reviews that it feels a bit derivative of It or even Stranger Things, but I digress. It may have some inspiration or a few similar beats to one of those, but it doesn't feel like a rip-off in any way.

The characters are typically 80's, and the exorcism passages are obviously reminiscent of the magnum opus of exorcisms: 'The Exorcist' while adding at the end a bit of a unique tongue-in-cheek touch, but the difference to that one is that 'My Best Friend's Exorcism' has a lot of heart. At its core is the story of two girls and their everlasting friendship, and I think the author did a great job with that.

The story goes from less to more in a slow-burn way that, in the end, connects everything perfectly making it a very pleasant read experience.

It's my third book from Grady Hendrix, and I'm officially a fan. There may have been a difference when it comes to 'The Final Girl Support Group', but I definitely think he's one of the new voices in horror that should be bigger than it already is.
description: Abby and Gretchen have been best friends since fifth grade, when they bonded over a shared love of E.T., roller-skating parties, and scratch-and-sniff stickers. But when they arrive at high school, things change. Gretchen begins to act….different. And as the strange coincidences and bizarre behavior start to pile up, Abby realizes there’s only one possible explanation: Gretchen, her favorite person in the world, has a demon living inside her. And Abby is not about to let anyone or anything come between her and her best friend. With help from some unlikely allies, Abby embarks on a quest to save Gretchen. But is their friendship powerful enough to beat the devil?

title: A Court of Wings and Ruin (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #3)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
Now THAT was a wild ride.

As I've previously said, ACOTAR as a series is my least favorite one in Sarah J. Mass's catalog. And I think it still is since it took me 3 whole books to make me fall in love with the world and its characters.

But man, I'm now in love with it.

It is an old book, so I won't dig deep in it since everyone read it before me, but I just loved the epicness that transpired through the page from the very start. Feyre? Amazing! Rhys? The best male character from any SJM book. Nesta? Badass. The whole gang? Incredible.

It definitely is more of a character-driven book, even when it has a lot of plot to cover, but you know what needs to happen and mostly how it's going to happen, so the surprises are not the biggest draw here, but the characters are. And that's why scenes like the High Fae reunion feel iconic because they can take the spotlight and shine.

But, because of this, many of the things from the plot that I cared about, were not my favorite, and you can feel the deus ex machina and the "you know he/she won't die" sensation a few too many times, making it all feel safe for everyone involved. And that happened as well in the 'Throne of Glass' final book: not a single MC died in the supposedly "biggest war ever faced", lowering the stakes and the danger of what is happening.

It's not that I want every single character to suffer and die, but claiming that hundreds of fighters died, but not a single one of *our* characters did, takes me out of the story because it's just not believable in the context of the book.

I know that this is not the end of the series and something shocking regarding what I just said may come up later, but let's be realistic... originally, this book was going to be the end and we are now in the cash grab part of ACOTAR. Not a criticism, just a fact. And I'm ready for it.
description:
The epic third novel in the #1 bestselling Court of Thorns and Roses series by global phenomenon Sarah J. Maas.

Feyre has returned to the Spring Court, determined to gather information on Tamlin's actions and learn what she can about the invading king threatening to bring her land to its knees. But to do so she must play a deadly game of deceit. One slip could bring doom not only for Feyre, but for everything-and everyone-she holds dear.

As war bears down upon them all, Feyre endeavors to take her place amongst the High Fae of the land, balancing her struggle to master her powers-both magical and political-and her love for her court and family. Amidst these struggles, Feyre and Rhysand must decide whom to trust amongst the cunning and lethal High Lords, and hunt for allies in unexpected places.

In this thrilling third book in the #1 bestselling series from Sarah J. Maas, the fate of Feyre's world is at stake as armies grapple for power over the one thing that could destroy it.

title: The Hand on the Wall (Truly Devious, #3)
author: Maureen Johnson
review:
And then this mystery comes to an end.

I’m a little sad about finishing this series, but I think that a trilogy regarding the same mystery was more than enough.

Like I said in my review of ‘The Vanishing Stair’, the Truly Devious series could have worked so much better as a duology than it was as a trilogy, mostly because the mystery, while interesting, was not as expanding or deep as a trilogy is supposed to be.

Now, talking about this book in particular, I think it was, for the most part, a satisfying ending to the whole series. The whodunnit was resolved kind of anti climatically but the journey to get there was worth it. Stevie as always was an amazing MC, and the whole set of SC was charming and had some funny interactions. I admit I warmed up a bit to David in this book, but I can’t help to think that his relationship with Stevie is not healthy since it was based on secrets from the beginning and they continue to be mean and rude to each other until they just kind of forgave each other for the sake of plot in the last 70 pages. Not my favorite YA romance at all.

Now, the chapters in the past, just like in previous books, were so much more interesting than the ones in the present, and it’s a shame that the whole mystery wasn’t bigger so that we could explore more about those characters and their lives. That’s a bummer.

Another bummer? I have to say that it was such a wasted opportunity that Maureen Johnson really decided to let the Truly Devious part of the plot become a prank. It felt a bit like a deus ex machina situation, since it was supposed to be this huge thing, and by the end it was literally just a joke. Was that really the original plan for the series?
And also, the fact that whole chapters were dedicated to this couple of characters that had absolutely no follow up after their appearance on the second book and a cameo on the third one, or any sort of involvement in the mystery was, to me, the worst part of this series and a huge disappointment.

Taking in consideration the whole trilogy, it’s a solid 4 star series, so not bad.. but I’m just a bit disappointed because the first book was amazing and the rest of them subpar.
description: New York Times bestselling author Maureen Johnson delivers the witty and pulse-pounding conclusion to the Truly Devious series as Stevie Bell solves the mystery that has haunted Ellingham Academy for over 75 years. Now available in paperback. Ellingham Academy must be cursed. Three people are now dead. One, a victim of either a prank gone wrong or a murder. Another, dead by misadventure. And now, an accident in Burlington has claimed another life. All three in the wrong place at the wrong time. All at the exact moment of Stevie’s greatest triumph . . . She knows who Truly Devious is. She’s solved it. The greatest case of the century. At least, she thinks she has. With this latest tragedy, it’s hard to concentrate on the past. Not only has someone died in town, but David disappeared of his own free will and is up to something. Stevie is sure that somehow—somehow—all these things connect. The three deaths in the present. The deaths in the past. The missing Alice Ellingham and the missing David Eastman. Somewhere in this place of riddles and puzzles there must be answers. Then another accident occurs as a massive storm heads toward Vermont. This is too much for the parents and administrators. Ellingham Academy is evacuated. Obviously, it’s time for Stevie to do something stupid. It’s time to stay on the mountain and face the storm—and a murderer. In the tantalizing finale to the Truly Devious trilogy, New York Times bestselling author Maureen Johnson expertly tangles her dual narrative threads and ignites an explosive end for all who’ve walked through Ellingham Academy. Praise for the Truly Devious “Readers, hang there’s one more round to come, and if the signs are right, it’ll be to die for.” — Publishers Weekly (starred review) “The Agatha Christie-like ecosystem pairs with lacerating contemporary wit, and alternating past and present scenes makes for a multilayered, modern detective story.” — New York Times Book Review “Remember the first time reading Harry Potter and knowing it was special? There’s that same sense of magic in the introduction of teen Sherlock-in-training Stevie Bell.” — USA Today (four stars) “Be still, my Agatha-Christie-loving beating heart.” —Bustle

title: The Vanishing Stair
author: Maureen Johnson
review:
Definitely not as good as the first one, The Vanishing Stair DOES suffer from the middle book syndrome, but it benefits from having a killer ending that propels the mystery forward and that puts Stevie and her gang one stop closer to discover the truth behind the kidnapping and murder at hand.

Being honest, the first 200 pages weren't doing it for me, I was easily distracted and even if I wasn't forcing myself to continue, it wasn't nearly as engrossing as 'Truly Devious' was and that is disappointing. I literally could see how the plot was stretched out because chapters went on and on, and nothing was happening. Yes, Stevie was following some leads and doing some research, but it wasn't until halfway through the book that Ellie's body was found and I felt that we were actually going somewhere.

Also, can we please stop romanticizing toxic people? David is literally the worst character in this entire series and that's because he's following the usual pattern of a love interest guy in a YA series by being mysterious and charming, but at the same time mistreating our main character while she falls for him for no reason whatsoever. It's just so late 00's that is not fun anymore. Especially in a book that doesn't needs it.

Now I'm really hoping that the Truly Devious aspect of the mystery recovers some momentum or importance in the third book because it was seriously mistreated in here. It's the name of the first book and of the series, I'll be really insulted if, in fact, the whole message thing was just a prank-gone-wrong from a couple of characters that I don't really care much about.

Anyway, I'm still excited for the next book in which I know the case is resolved and I have big hopes for that.
3.5 stars rounded up to 4.
description: All Stevie Bell wanted was to find the key to the Ellingham mystery, but instead she found her classmate dead. And while she solved that murder, the crimes of the past are still waiting in the dark. Just as Stevie feels she’s on the cusp of putting it together, her parents pull her out of Ellingham academy.For her own safety they say. She must move past this obsession with crime. Now that Stevie’s away from the school of topiaries and secret tunnels, and her strange and endearing friends, she begins to feel disconnected from the rest of the world. At least she won’t have to see David anymore. David, who she kissed. David, who lied to her about his identity—son of despised politician Edward King. Then King himself arrives at her house to offer a He will bring Stevie back to Ellingham immediately. In return, she must play nice with David. King is in the midst of a campaign and can’t afford his son stirring up trouble. If Stevie’s at school, David will stay put.The tantalizing riddles behind the Ellingham murders are still waiting to be unraveled, and Stevie knows she’s so close. But the path to the truth has more twists and turns than she can imagine—and moving forward involves hurting someone she cares for. In New York Times bestselling author Maureen Johnson’s second novel of the Truly Devious series, nothing is free, and someone will pay for the truth with their life.

title: Once Upon a Broken Heart (Once Upon a Broken Heart, #1)
author: Stephanie Garber
review:
A better-than-expected 4.5 stars.

So much better than Caraval and I’m actually intrigued to know what happens next.

I can now forgive Stephanie Garber after disappointing me with Legendary and Finale.
description:
For as long as she can remember, Evangeline Fox has believed in true love and happy endings... until she learns that the love of her life will marry another.

Desperate to stop the wedding and to heal her wounded heart, Evangeline strikes a deal with the charismatic, but wicked, Prince of Hearts. In exchange for his help, he asks for three kisses, to be given at the time and place of his choosing.

But after Evangeline’s first promised kiss, she learns that bargaining with an immortal is a dangerous game ― and that the Prince of Hearts wants far more from her than she’d pledged. He has plans for Evangeline, plans that will either end in the greatest happily ever after, or the most exquisite tragedy.

title: The Titan's Curse (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #3)
author: Rick Riordan
review:
Another solid entry to the Percy Jackson series, and things are starting to feel a bit formulaic, aren’t they?

I’m still liking it, they are super quick and easy to read and some jokes land really well, but they’re also really… predictable

I know this is an old middle grade series and I can’t be that harsh because of the demographic it’s directed to. I believe that these books are one of the reasons of why many people started to read. That’s powerful and I can see why.

There’s not a lot that I can add that haven’t been said before, I’ll just say that I’m ready for the fourth book where I hope things get a bit more exciting. There has been so many build up regarding the prophecy and it’s time for it to arrive.
description:
When Percy Jackson receives an urgent distress call from his friend Grover, he immediately prepares for battle. He knows he'll need his powerful demigod allies at his side; his trusty bronze sword, Riptide; and... a ride from his mom.

The demigods race to the rescue to find that Grover has made an important discovery: two powerful half-bloods, whose parentage is unknown. But that's not all that awaits them. The Titan lord Kronos has set up a devious trap, and the young heroes have just fallen prey.

Hilarious and action-packed, this third adventure in the series finds Percy faced with his most dangerous challenge yet--the chilling prophecy of the Titan's curse.

title: The Sea of Monsters (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #2)
author: Rick Riordan
review:
This might be an unpopular opinion, but I liked this one better than the first one.

I don't know if it was because I didn't even knew what happened in Sea of Monsters, compared to Lightning Thief where we all know what happens, but even though this book was mostly a subplot, I couldn't help to like it.

The characters are better, the narration is funnier and the addition of Tyson is amazing, he's such a sweet big thing and I just fell for him.

Of course since this is Middle Grade, there's not much depth and everything is just glossed over, but every once in a while a book like this is just what I need.

A solid 4.5 read to me.
description:
The heroic son of Poseidon makes an action-packed comeback in the second must-read installment of Rick Riordan's amazing young readers series. Starring Percy Jackson, a "half blood" whose mother is human and whose father is the God of the Sea, Riordan's series combines cliffhanger adventure and Greek mythology lessons that results in true page-turners that get better with each installment.

In this episode, The Sea of Monsters, Percy sets out to retrieve the Golden Fleece before his summer camp is destroyed, surpassing the first book's drama and setting the stage for more thrills to come.

title: Blood & Honey (Serpent & Dove, #2)
author: Shelby Mahurin
review:
So, for the first time since I started rating and reviewing books, I didn't felt pressured to like a book… I actually felt pressured to dislike it.

Okay, maybe I'm exaggerating, no one was telling me to hate it, but the common opinion for 'Blood & Honey' is that it is disappointing, boring and mostly filler. And while the latter is definitely true since we don't need 500+ pages for what happened in here, I actually quite liked it. And let me explain why:

First things first, I have to admit that while I enjoyed the first book, I wasn't BLOWN away by it like many other people were. To me, the world building was a bit confusing, the romance while fun, also was really… I don't know, unrealistic, and it overall just was an OK story. Nothing groundbreaking. So starting from there, my expectations for the second book weren't the highest (unlike many other readers who were really anticipating this sequel).

And that's why I actually enjoyed it. Did a lot happen? Not at all, it was mostly our old characters going from Point A to Point B and C trying to recruit allies. I don't usually like these type of storylines, but surprisingly, I enjoyed it. I think that all the characters that were introduced here were far more interesting than any of our OGs: Claud is, hands-down, the best character in the series, La Voisin actually intrigued me (contrary to Morgane who is just pure evil and that's not really fun). Likewise, I found some captivating conflict within Blaise, Ismay and Gabrielle had much more depth than some OGs in fewer pages, and so on.

So that's why for the rest, unfortunately there's not much I can say: Ansel was just his weak and scared old self, Coco was there just to rescue Lou and the gang every 5 chapters or so, Beau is probably the most improved character in the bunch, but that's because he was mostly a presence on the first one and Madame Labelle… well she's fine. And I think that's the problem with them. They are doing nothing, but is that any different from the first book? I don't think so. So that's why it didn't really bother me.

Now, I've read a lot of reviews saying that Lou and Reid were just fighting throughout the whole book and that it became tedious because they wanted their banter and the sexiness back, and it's true, they went through a rough patch here, but I also found their situation far more intriguing than if they were living a happily ever after-esque situation. C'mon, Reid was a witchunter who hated magic, and Lou is a witch (who is losing her mind, btw), and all of a sudden, he discovers that he's a witch and can use magic. Did you really think that it would be easy for him to just accept it? Imagine it. Yes, we could have had scenes with Lou teaching him magic, and that would have probably been nice, but I don't think it would have been true or believable.

I may be in the minority, but I really appreciated that Shelby Mahurin didn't take the easy and fan service route by glossing over what happened at the end of the first book, just so the fans could have their romantic banter here. Big things happened to both Lou and Reid, so for them just to conveniently forget or don't give enough thought about who they are, and their situation and what they feel for each other once the honeymoon phase passed was much more realistic.

Now, is it boring? I think it depends. With this book, I discovered that I actually enjoy these middle books in fantasy trilogies, because I feel like we can really get to know the world without the pressure of getting to know the characters for the first time or the magic system or that we're running towards a big finale. It can breathe.

It happened here, and also in the Shadow and Bone series, where I enjoyed the second one more than the first, and while I don't think that 'Blood & Honey' is better than 'Serpent & Dove', I do think that people over exaggerated their hatred towards this one.

So, yeah, that is my opinion, I can't rate it any lower than 4 better-than-expected stars.
description:
The hotly anticipated sequel to the New York Times and IndieBound bestseller Serpent & Dove—packed with even steamier romance and darker magic—is perfect for fans of Sarah J. Maas.

After narrowly escaping death at the hands of the Dames Blanches, Lou, Reid, Coco, and Ansel are on the run from coven, kingdom, and church—fugitives with nowhere to hide.

To elude the scores of witches and throngs of chasseurs at their heels, Lou and Reid need allies. Strong ones. But protection comes at a price, and the group is forced to embark on separate quests to build their forces. As Lou and Reid try to close the widening rift between them, the dastardly Morgane baits them in a lethal game of cat and mouse that threatens to destroy something worth more than any coven.

title: My Sister, the Serial Killer
author: Oyinkan Braithwaite
review:
Mostly boring and full of side plots that I didn’t cared for.
It starts amazing, but it quickly becomes inconsequential, predictable and not very interesting.
description:
When Korede's dinner is interrupted one night by a distress call from her sister, Ayoola, she knows what's expected of her: bleach, rubber gloves, nerves of steel and a strong stomach. This'll be the third boyfriend Ayoola's dispatched in, quote, self-defence and the third mess that her lethal little sibling has left Korede to clear away. She should probably go to the police for the good of the menfolk of Nigeria, but she loves her sister and, as they say, family always comes first. Until, that is, Ayoola starts dating the doctor where Korede works as a nurse. Korede's long been in love with him, and isn't prepared to see him wind up with a knife in his back: but to save one would mean sacrificing the other...

My Sister, the Serial Killer is a blackly comic novel about how blood is thicker - and more difficult to get out of the carpet - than water...

title: Iron Widow (Iron Widow, #1)
author: Xiran Jay Zhao
review:
Someone has taken their love with Daenerys Targaryen in the final season of GOT one step too far.

I'm just kidding, but wow… this book is amazing. I don't know why I was actually expecting this to be a fantasy book, when it totally is a sci-fi. Furthermore, I was surprised in a good way, and that was a constant throughout the whole book, which was refreshing.

Spoilers ahead.

During the first couple of chapters I was 100% sure about what was going to happen at the end, but Xiran Jay Zhao said “You don't know half of it” and she committed to it. It was so wild to actually see our main girl's desire fulfilled not even halfway through the story because that's not usually how this books go, that I was so glued to the pages.

End of spoilers.

Now, I've read some reviews about how Zetian's motivation and drive might be unrealistic given the context of the story, but I digress. If not enough women in real life were like her (in the sense of female empowerment and wanting a change) the world would be even less fair when it comes to gender equality than it already is. We have still so much work to be done, but I don't think that any girl like Zetian who may exist in real life needs more motivation to break the status quo that just wanting to break free and live how she wants to live: without fear, judgement or condescend.

But coming back to the book, it definitely elevates because of its characters. Zetian was so amazing at being a badass girl who discovered that she could also be loved by a man who doesn't look down at her, but sees her as his equal, while Shimin and Yhizi proved that not because a character is the “male love interest” must be this alpha, possessive, borderline psycho man who seems to abound in YA and NA. They can be caring, fun and light-hearted, but still brave.

Also, the exploration of polyamorous relationships, while brief, was also so cute, believable and heartwarming. Why is this not a thing in more books? It's so much more engaging than a love triangle.

Anyway, I really enjoyed this book. Maybe the last part of it was a bit rushed and… let's call it easy, but I don't think that it diminishes the awesomeness of the whole thing.
description:
The boys of Huaxia dream of pairing up with girls to pilot Chrysalises, giant transforming robots that can battle the mecha aliens that lurk beyond the Great Wall. It doesn't matter that the girls often die from the mental strain.

When 18-year-old Zetian offers herself up as a concubine-pilot, it's to assassinate the ace male pilot responsible for her sister's death. But she gets her vengeance in a way nobody expected—she kills him through the psychic link between pilots and emerges from the cockpit unscathed. She is labeled an Iron Widow, a much-feared and much-silenced kind of female pilot who can sacrifice boys to power up Chrysalises instead.​

To tame her unnerving yet invaluable mental strength, she is paired up with Li Shimin, the strongest and most controversial male pilot in Huaxia​. But now that Zetian has had a taste of power, she will not cower so easily. She will miss no opportunity to leverage their combined might and infamy to survive attempt after attempt on her life, until she can figure out exactly why the pilot system works in its misogynist way—and stop more girls from being sacrificed.

title: The Burning Girls
author: C.J. Tudor
review:
I don't even remember much about what happened in this book.

I won't lie and say that I hated it, but it was underwhelming in many aspects. The mystery? Unnecessarily complicated and, at the end of the day, it didn't even need to be that way. After everything was said and done, apparently THE mystery was comprised of TWO mysteries... meh.

The characters? I liked the two main characters, but the twists concerning them were predictable. Perhaps, if you're not a thriller reader, one of them could throw you for a loop, but if you read thrillers, you'll guess this one in a second.

Also, do we care about any of the SC? I didn't, and the whole reveal depended on one of them who got almost no screen time (page time? read time?) to make me invested. A shame.

Now, I didn't hate it. I had a mostly OK time with this one, and maybe it was just a miss for the author. If you're curious, check it out, just don't expect to find the next big thriller here.
description:
An unconventional vicar moves to a remote corner of the English countryside, only to discover a community haunted by death and disappearances both past and present--and intent on keeping its dark secrets--in this explosive, unsettling thriller from acclaimed author C. J. Tudor.

Welcome to Chapel Croft. Five hundred years ago, eight protestant martyrs were burned at the stake here. Thirty years ago, two teenage girls disappeared without a trace. And two months ago, the vicar of the local parish killed himself.

Reverend Jack Brooks, a single parent with a fourteen-year-old daughter and a heavy conscience, arrives in the village hoping to make a fresh start and find some peace. Instead, Jack finds a town mired in secrecy and a strange welcome package: an old exorcism kit and a note quoting scripture. "But there is nothing covered up that will not be revealed and hidden that will not be known."

The more Jack and her daughter Flo get acquainted with the town and its strange denizens, the deeper they are drawn into their rifts, mysteries, and suspicions. And when Flo is troubled by strange sightings in the old chapel, it becomes apparent that there are ghosts here that refuse to be laid to rest.

But uncovering the truth can be deadly in a village where everyone has something to protect, everyone has links with the village's bloody past, and no one trusts an outsider.

title: My Heart Is a Chainsaw (The Indian Lake Trilogy, #1)
author: Stephen Graham Jones
review:
This one was hard to rate, but after considering it, I think it deserves 3 sometimes-slow-sometimes-amazing stars.

Why was it hard? Mostly because it starts slow, and I'm not kidding, this is easily the slowest-paced book I've ever read. 150 pages of confusion and not understanding what's happening, and adding boredom to it, doesn't translate into a good read.

I read some reviews about people complaining about the same thing, and they all said that the pace picked up around the 75% mark. I think they're wrong, it's actually around the 50% one that you finally get the hang of what's going on and events start to happen. For some, it may be too late, but for me... I wanted to see what happened, so I persevered. And I'm glad I did.

The mystery does pick up, and some chilly descriptions and situations made me consider (for a moment) grading up this whole book to a 4-star read. I was having a great time until the climax. It's not that it was bad, but I don't think the book gave any real indication about what ultimately happens.

Spoilers in the following paragraph.

Yes, this is a slasher based book, and slashers are silly most of the time, but we had a mystery grounded on real characters and events, not paranormal ones, so that's why it doesn't click with me, why all of a sudden we have a ghost (?) as our big reveal. It was the biggest letdown in the history of slasher and book reveals I've ever had.

So, just because of that, I can't rate with 4-stars. I'm sorry, I tried to give it a few days to see if I could warm up to it, but I couldn't.

Will I read the sequel? I think it depends on the reviews, mostly.
description:
You won’t find a more hardcore eighties-slasher-film fan than high school senior Jade Daniels. And you won’t find a place less supportive of girls who wear torn T-shirts and too much eyeliner than Proofrock, nestled eight thousand feet up a mountain in Idaho, alongside Indian Lake, home to both Camp Blood – site of a massacre fifty years ago – and, as of this summer, Terra Nova, a second-home celebrity Camelot being carved out of a national forest.

That’s not the only thing that’s getting carved up, though – this, Jade knows, is the start of a slasher. But what kind? Who’s wearing the mask? Jade’s got an encyclopedic recall of every horror movie on the shelf, but… will that help her survive? Can she get a final girl trained enough to stop all this from happening? Does she even want to?

Isn’t a slasher exactly what her hometown deserves?

This new novel by the New York Times bestselling author of The Only Good Indians, Stephen Graham Jones, called “one of our most talented living writers” by Tommy Orange, explores the changing landscape of the West through his distinct voice of sharp humor and prophetic violence.

Go up the mountain to Proofrock. See if you’ve got what it takes – see if your heart, too, might be a chainsaw.

title: The Sun Down Motel
author: Simone St. James
review:
The Sun Down Motel was a book that I was excited to get into. It seemed to be scary, and chilling, and it had a mystery-solving endgame that I was hoping would satisfy my craving for a horror novel.

It did, up to a certain point. While the ghosts in the story spooked me a bit, the whole mystery part of the book was too convenient, especially when the resolution came. I don't recall that much about it, since I read it a few weeks ago, but I do remember that the characters arrived at conclusions seemingly out of nowhere, not because they were doing their detective work right.

Am I going to read another book from Simone St. James? Probably some time along the way, but I'm not itching for another.
description:
Something hasn't been right at the roadside Sun Down Motel for a very long time, and Carly Kirk is about to find out why in this chilling new novel from the New York Times bestselling and award-winning author of The Broken Girls.

Upstate New York, 1982. Viv Delaney wants to move to New York City, and to help pay for it she takes a job as the night clerk at the Sun Down Motel in Fell, New York. But something isnʼt right at the motel, something haunting and scary.

Upstate New York, 2017. Carly Kirk has never been able to let go of the story of her aunt Viv, who mysteriously disappeared from the Sun Down before she was born. She decides to move to Fell and visit the motel, where she quickly learns that nothing has changed since 1982. And she soon finds herself ensnared in the same mysteries that claimed her aunt.

title: Fairest of All (Villains, #1)
author: Serena Valentino
review: Short and sweet, I mostly enjoyed this story even if it felt a bit like fan fiction and the bummer of feeling like the ending was rushed!
description:
For anyone who’s seen Walt Disney’s Snow White, you’ll know that the Wicked Queen is one evil woman! After all, it’s not everyone who wants to cut out their teenage step-daughter’s heart and have it delivered back in a locked keepsake box. (And even if this sort of thing is a common urge, we don’t know many people who have acted upon it.)

Now, for the first time, we’ll examine the life of the Wicked Queen and find out just what it is that makes her so nasty. Here’s a hint: the creepy-looking man in the magic mirror is not just some random spooky visage—and he just might have something to do with the Queen’s wicked ways!

title: The Hawthorne Legacy (The Inheritance Games, #2)
author: Jennifer Lynn Barnes
review:
A 3.5 star read to me.

Definitely not as good or exciting as the first one, but it still has a lot of charm. I think this book suffers from second book syndrome, because even though a lot of reveals are spread in here, with one book left in the series, it’s kind of unsatisfying to know that we have more secrets to uncover that will probably debunk a lot of what happens here.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s an interesting plot the one that the author built for this series, and I don’t mind suspending my disbelief for the sake of having a good time, but there has been a lot of red herrings already that I think I almost don’t care about the secrets anymore. It’s a bit over complicated at this point, specially because the main mystery it’s not that big of a deal and I don’t see why Tobias did ALL of this, even with that reasoning thrown in about “being a Hawthorne”

We ultimately care because of the characters, Avery and Jameson are amazing together, and I don’t really think there are a lot of Grayson shippers out there, I don’t think even think the author is really trying to make us believe that Grayson + Avery is a real possibility. The leaning towards Jameson is really evident.

Anyway, I liked it, I’ll be reading the third one, but this could have been a lot better as a duology
description:
Intrigue, riches, and romance abound in this thrilling sequel to the New York Times bestselling The Inheritance Games perfect for fans of Karen McManus and Holly Jackson.

The Inheritance Games ended with a bombshell, and now heiress Avery Grambs has to pick up the pieces and find the man who might hold the answers to all of her questions - including why Tobias Hawthorne left his entire fortune to Avery, a virtual stranger, rather than to his own daughters or grandsons.

Thanks to a DNA test, Avery knows that she's not a Hawthorne by blood, but clues pile up hinting at a deeper connection to the family than she had ever imagined. As the mystery grows and the plot thickens, Grayson and Jameson, the enigmatic and magnetic Hawthorne grandsons, continue to pull Avery in different directions. And there are threats lurking around every corner, as adversaries emerge who will stop at nothing to see Avery out of the picture - by any means necessary.

With nonstop action, aspirational jet-setting, family intrigue, swoonworthy romance, and billions of dollars hanging in the balance, The Hawthorne Legacy will thrill Jennifer Lynn Barnes fans and new readers alike.

title: The Southern Book Club's Guide to Slaying Vampires
author: Grady Hendrix
review:
If Desperate Housewives had a child with American Horror Story, this book would have been the result.

And what a delightful surprise it was.

Coming off a few weeks ago from the letdown my first experience with Grady Hendrix was, I wasn’t all that excited for ‘The Southern Book Club’s Guide to Slaying Vampires’, but there is a reason why I saw this book regarded as his best work and it shows.

It IS scary, it’s fresh and while a bit silly, it really critiques the sexism and racism that’s still prevalent to this day in American society in a way that doesn’t feel preachy, but by making you feel angry and desperate.

It’s not perfect, especially in its resolution: the climax feels rushed and the ending a bit too easy and anti climactic for my taste. Also, for some reason there were some funny bits in the “final battle” scene that felt weird because the book was not presented as a satire at any point. We really feel throughout the story the fear and power that James represents, and making him a bit of a buffoon on the last part was weird.

Despite those little details, I had a blast while reading it and I would really recommend it: some parts were so tense that I don’t think any other book has made me feel that anxious, and just because of that, I can forgive some things.
description:
Fried Green Tomatoes and Steel Magnolias meet Dracula in this Southern-flavored supernatural thriller set in the '90s about a women's book club that must protect its suburban community from a mysterious and handsome stranger who turns out to be a blood-sucking fiend.

Patricia Campbell had always planned for a big life, but after giving up her career as a nurse to marry an ambitious doctor and become a mother, Patricia's life has never felt smaller. The days are long, her kids are ungrateful, her husband is distant, and her to-do list is never really done. The one thing she has to look forward to is her book club, a group of Charleston mothers united only by their love for true-crime and suspenseful fiction. In these meetings, they're more likely to discuss the FBI's recent siege of Waco as much as the ups and downs of marriage and motherhood.

But when an artistic and sensitive stranger moves into the neighborhood, the book club's meetings turn into speculation about the newcomer. Patricia is initially attracted to him, but when some local children go missing, she starts to suspect the newcomer is involved. She begins her own investigation, assuming that he's a Jeffrey Dahmer or Ted Bundy. What she uncovers is far more terrifying, and soon she—and her book club—are the only people standing between the monster they've invited into their homes and their unsuspecting community.

title: People We Meet on Vacation
author: Emily Henry
review: One of the quickest reads of my life - Loved it🤩
description:
Two best friends. Ten summer trips. One last chance to fall in love.
