Poppy and Alex. Alex and Poppy. They have nothing in common. She’s a wild child; he wears khakis. She has insatiable wanderlust; he prefers to stay home with a book. And somehow, ever since a fateful car share home from college many years ago, they are the very best of friends. For most of the year they live far apart—she’s in New York City and he’s in their small hometown—but every summer for a decade, they have taken one glorious week of vacation together.

Until two years ago, when they ruined everything. They haven’t spoken since.

Poppy has everything she should want, but she’s stuck in a rut. When someone asks when she was last truly happy, she knows without a doubt it was on that ill-fated final trip with Alex. And so, she decides to convince her best friend to take one more vacation together—lay everything on the table, make it all right. Miraculously, he agrees.

Now she has a week to fix everything. If only she can get around the one big truth that has always stood quietly in the middle of their seemingly perfect relationship. What could possibly go wrong?

title: Project Hail Mary
author: Andy Weir
review: Rocky tqmmm
description:
Ryland Grace is the sole survivor on a desperate, last-chance mission—and if he fails, humanity and the earth itself will perish.

Except that right now, he doesn’t know that. He can’t even remember his own name, let alone the nature of his assignment or how to complete it.

All he knows is that he’s been asleep for a very, very long time. And he’s just been awakened to find himself millions of miles from home, with nothing but two corpses for company.

His crewmates dead, his memories fuzzily returning, Ryland realizes that an impossible task now confronts him. Hurtling through space on this tiny ship, it’s up to him to puzzle out an impossible scientific mystery—and conquer an extinction-level threat to our species.

And with the clock ticking down and the nearest human being light-years away, he’s got to do it all alone.

Or does he?

title: Fable (The World of the Narrows, #1)
author: Adrienne Young
review:
Talk about a book that goes from less to more.

During the first 80 pages or so I was close to give up on this book because I found it confusing, with lots of nautical words that I needed to look up on my phone and a slow start, but thankfully I persisted. It doesn't have the biggest plot, the most interesting characters or the most absorbing setting, but it is a pleasant and fun story about a crew of traders/pirates who become a family of sorts due to some circumstances that I won't spoil.

Now, I do feel (and this is something I've never said about a book) that 'Fable' should have been longer. Yes, even with 350 pages and a slow start, the book feels short, mostly because of the lack of character building that the crew receives and the easy resolution to every single thing that happened. A character got stabbed? No worries, by the next chapter he or she will be stitched up and ready to go. Does our crew need to go on an almost impossible quest that few crews would dare to adventure on? Thats OK, our heroine and her friends are up to the task and they'll solve in the next 10 pages.

Everything was so easy that the stakes during the whole book were really low. That's not bad, but 'Fable' is being advertised as an adventure novel, make it feel that way. Also, I think everything would have had a bigger impact if the author gave us more insight on the side characters. Fable, Willa and maybe West are explored throughout the novel, and we do get to know them, but the rest of the people in here are mere interchangeable names that would have benefited from more background. Perhaps this is solved on the second book, but I think that's the cause that the ending while intended to be shocking was just like... oh, that happened!

Based on my feelings and on the fact that I did enjoyed it, I can't rate it below 4 stars. It is good, but I hate to feel that there was SO much potential in this to become an amazing big novel, and that maybe its scope was too short.
description:
For seventeen-year-old Fable, the daughter of the most powerful trader in the Narrows, the sea is the only home she has ever known. It’s been four years since the night she watched her mother drown during an unforgiving storm. The next day her father abandoned her on a legendary island filled with thieves and little food. To survive she must keep to herself, learn to trust no one, and rely on the unique skills her mother taught her. The only thing that keeps her going is the goal of getting off the island, finding her father, and demanding her rightful place beside him and his crew. To do so Fable enlists the help of a young trader named West to get her off the island and across the Narrows to her father.

But her father’s rivalries and the dangers of his trading enterprise have only multiplied since she last saw him, and Fable soon finds that West isn't who he seems. Together, they will have to survive more than the treacherous storms that haunt the Narrows if they're going to stay alive.

Welcome to a world made dangerous by the sea and by those who wish to profit from it. Where a young girl must find her place and her family while trying to survive in a world built for men. Fable takes you on a spectacular journey filled with romance, intrigue, and adventure.

A newer edition of ISBN 9781250254368 can be found here.

title: Six Crimson Cranes (Six Crimson Cranes, #1)
author: Elizabeth Lim
review:
Do you want a book that definitely lives up to its hype? This is the one for you.

Six Crimson Cranes was not what I thought it would be, but I don’t mean that in a negative way. Quite the opposite, it was amazing and so much more.

Elizabeth Lim really created an enormous and amazing world straight out of a fairytale and made it her own by allowing her characters to really explore it. I noticed that it’s fairly common for a fantasy book to have this big and complicated map on the first couple of pages and have its characters only visiting two or three locations for the whole book. Well, I just loved how Lim allowed us to get to know this world and its inhabitants at the same time Shiori did without ever making it complicated or tedious.

Yes, it does have a couple of pacing issues, especially once you’re between the pages 250 and 350, and some of the twists were kind of predictable, but I just couldn’t help but fall for this one.

It was my first fantasy book inspired by Asian mythology, but I’m sure it won’t be the last.

I’m so excited for the second part of this duology, but please Elizabeth, just let Shiori and Takkan kiss!
description:
A princess in exile, the boy she left at the altar, six enchanted cranes, and a dragon from the deepest sea.

Shiori, the only princess of Kiata, has a secret. Forbidden magic runs through her veins. Normally she conceals it well, but on the morning of her betrothal ceremony, Shiori loses control. At first, her mistake seems like a stroke of luck, forestalling the wedding she never wanted, but it also catches the attention of Raikama, her stepmother.

Raikama has dark magic of her own, and she banishes the young princess, turning her brothers into cranes, and warning Shiori that she must speak of it to no one: for with every word that escapes her lips, one of her brothers will die.

Peniless, voiceless, and alone, Shiori searches for her brothers, and, on her journey, uncovers a conspiracy to overtake the throne--a conspiracy more twisted and deceitful, more cunning and complex, than even Raikama's betrayal. Only Shiori can set the kingdom to rights, but to do so she must place her trust in the very boy she fought so hard not to marry. And she must embrace the magic she's been taught all her life to contain--no matter what it costs her.

From the author of Spin the Dawn comes a breathtakingly original fantasy inspired by East Asian folklore and perfect for fans of Leigh Bardugo or Tomi Adeyemi.

title: Good Girl, Bad Blood (A Good Girl's Guide to Murder, #2)
author: Holly  Jackson
review: So much better than the first one!
description:
Pip is not a detective anymore.

With the help of Ravi Singh, she released a true-crime podcast about the murder case they solved together last year. The podcast has gone viral, yet Pip insists her investigating days are behind her.

But she will have to break that promise when someone she knows goes missing. Jamie Reynolds has disappeared, on the very same night the town hosted a memorial for the sixth-year anniversary of the deaths of Andie Bell and Sal Singh.

The police won't do anything about it. And if they won't look for Jamie then Pip will, uncovering more of her town's dark secrets along the way... and this time everyone is listening. But will she find him before it's too late?

title: Ace of Spades
author: Faridah Àbíké-Íyímídé
review:
What a powerful read ‘Ace of Spades’ was.

A really outstanding, creepy and very important debut that may give the impression of being a Gossip Girl or Pretty Little Liars ripoff, but that ultimately becomes so much more.

And it really is a deadly, complex and horrible situation the one that our main characters go through. In hindsight, probably the “secrets” that they were keeping were not as big as the first half of the book made them feel, but it was what lurked beneath the surface of the Aces game that really notches up this book. Trust me, this is what other books and tv shows of the genre wanted and failed to be.

I won’t go into detail because of spoilers, but there were genuine gasps of shock coming out of me when the truth is revealed and everything clicks into place. Especially one betrayal which, I don’t know if I’m the only one who got heartbroken by it, but it hurt me.

The characters? Amazing. The story? Top notch. The ending? Maybe a bit too easy and happily ever after-ish (especially after the big deus ex machina that comes with it), but good overall.
description:
Gossip Girl meets Get Out in Ace of Spades, a YA contemporary thriller by debut author Faridah Àbíké-Íyímídé about two students, Devon & Chiamaka, and their struggles against an anonymous bully.

When two Niveus Private Academy students, Devon Richards and Chiamaka Adebayo, are selected to be part of the elite school’s senior class prefects, it looks like their year is off to an amazing start. After all, not only does it look great on college applications, but it officially puts each of them in the running for valedictorian, too.

Shortly after the announcement is made, though, someone who goes by Aces begins using anonymous text messages to reveal secrets about the two of them that turn their lives upside down and threaten every aspect of their carefully planned futures.

As Aces shows no sign of stopping, what seemed like a sick prank quickly turns into a dangerous game, with all the cards stacked against them. Can Devon and Chiamaka stop Aces before things become incredibly deadly?

With heart-pounding suspense and relevant social commentary comes a high-octane thriller from debut author Faridah Àbíké-Íyímídé.

title: Kingdom of the Wicked (Kingdom of the Wicked, #1)
author: Kerri Maniscalco
review:
What a fun little wicked time I had with this book.

I read some mixed reviews about ‘Kingdom of the Wicked’ that made nervous about it regarding its lack of romance, the convenience of some plot points and the confusing world building. And all those allegations are, in fact, true.

However, this book also blended a whodunnit mystery with fantasy, and by doing that, it completely grabbed me. Was it the best mystery I’ve ever read? Absolutely not. The best fantasy, maybe? Not really. But did I had a blast while reading it? I sure did.

Yes, the twist was kinda lame and predictable, some things about the curse and the motivations behind certain actions were unnecessarily confusing, and maybe the climax was nonexistent, but I sure had a great time while reading this and it was so addictive. I was just glued to the pages, and to me, that counts a lot.
description:
Two sisters.
One brutal murder.
A quest for vengeance that will unleash Hell itself...
And an intoxicating romance.

Emilia and her twin sister Vittoria are streghe - witches who live secretly among humans, avoiding notice and persecution. One night, Vittoria misses dinner service at the family's renowned Sicilian restaurant. Emilia soon finds the body of her beloved twin...desecrated beyond belief. Devastated, Emilia sets out to find her sister's killer and to seek vengeance at any cost—even if it means using dark magic that's been long forbidden.

Then Emilia meets Wrath, one of the Wicked—princes of Hell she has been warned against in tales since she was a child. Wrath claims to be on Emilia's side, tasked by his master with solving the series of women's murders on the island. But when it comes to the Wicked, nothing is as it seems...

title: We Need to Talk About Kevin
author: Lionel Shriver
review:
I can’t believe what I just read... one of the most powerful books I’ve ever laid my eyes on, with one of the most effective twists I’ve seen. So simple, yet so gut wrenching.

I really don’t have a lot to say, I just want to recommend it to everybody. The first few pages may take a bit to get used to because of the way it is written, but once you get past that, you can’t stop thinking about it.

Amazing stuff
description: Now a major motion picture by Lynne Ramsay, starring Tilda Swinton and John C. Reilly, Lionel Shriver’s resonant story of a mother’s unsettling quest to understand her teenage son’s deadly violence, her own ambivalence toward motherhood, and the explosive link between them reverberates with the haunting power of high hopes shattered by dark realities. Like Shriver’s charged and incisive later novels, including So Much for That and The Post-Birthday World, We Need to Talk About Kevin isa piercing, unforgettable, and penetrating exploration of violence, family ties, and responsibility, a book that the Boston Globe describes as “sometimes searing . . . [and] impossible to put down.”

title: The Thursday Murder Club (Thursday Murder Club, #1)
author: Richard Osman
review:
It becomes waaaay too convoluted by the end, but I had fun with it!

I’ll read the sequels
description:
In a peaceful retirement village, four unlikely friends meet up once a week to investigate unsolved murders.

But when a brutal killing takes place on their very doorstep, the Thursday Murder Club find themselves in the middle of their first live case. Elizabeth, Joyce, Ibrahim and Ron might be pushing eighty but they still have a few tricks up their sleeves.

Can our unorthodox but brilliant gang catch the killer before it's too late?

Alternate cover edition can be found here .

title: Truly Devious (Truly Devious, #1)
author: Maureen Johnson
review:
I will rate this little YA mystery with 5 amazing stars.

I'm not going to say that this book has a groundbreaking story or anything like that, but it was so refreshing to read a typical whodunnit made with such love and affection for the genre.

It is fun, it has a great mystery, Stevie is amazing, there was a big twist midway through the book that I definitely not see coming, and, the best of all things is that I have genuinely no idea of where this is going next or what is happening. And by being someone who has read a lot of thrillers and mysteries, that's a good sign. The flashbacks were actually so much more revealing that I expected them to be, so I guess we are still on the tip of the iceberg and there is so much more to reveal and to come, and that's really exciting.

And even if I'm not someone who is a fan of romantic subplots when they are not really necessary, the one that we find here is not as annoying as it might be in less capable hands. It may not add a lot to the overarching plot (at least yet) but it doesn't feel intrusive either, so, we're all good.

The only detail that bothered me, I think, is almost at the end, when Stevie connects a clue in the present about something that is mentioned in the past storyline and that makes totally no sense for Stevie to make that connection. Or at least it didn't made sense to me, perhaps in the next book this is further explored but that was a vague situation that popped me out of the book while reading it.

Anyway, my expectations for the rest of the series are high so let's hope that I won't be left disappointed.
description:
LOOK! A RIDDLE!

TIME FOR FUN!

SHOULD WE USE A ROPE OR GUN?

Ellingham Academy is a famous private school in Vermont, founded by an early twentieth century tycoon for the best and brightest students around. When Ellingham's wife and daughter were kidnapped, the only clue was a mocking riddle listing methods of murder, signed with the frightening pseudonym “Truly, Devious.” Their disappearance became one of the great unsolved crimes in history.

Many years later, true-crime aficionado Stevie Bell is set to begin her first year at the academy, and she is determined to solve this cold case. That is, she will solve it when she gets a grip on her demanding new school life and her housemates: the inventor, the novelist, the actor, the artist, and the jokester. But Truly Devious makes a surprise return. The past has crawled out of its grave, and someone has gotten away with murder. 

Truly Devious is the first novel in a murder-mystery trilogy by New York Times bestselling author Maureen Johnson.

title: Caraval (Caraval, #1)
author: Stephanie Garber
review:
Huh… who would have thought?

I need to be honest, when I started Caraval I wasn't really excited about it, since I thought it was going to be a silly YA fantasy novel with a sprinkle of romance on top of it.

And it was, but in a mostly pleasant, fun and interesting way. Also, I have to give credit where credit is due, this one was a grower. When I started it, it felt okay-ish. It had some things that were being developed differently than in other books of the sort, so it was promising, and that momentum just kept increasing until the 200-page mark, where I was enthralled. More than usual for a YA fantasy, especially a first one in a series where I tend to struggle, but Stephanie Garber's writing clicked with me in a really satisfying way.

There were some genuine surprises in here, as well. I'm glad that the whole “don't trust anything or anyone” motto was not just for creating a vibe. The book was actually full of reveals and surprises along the way, creating a nice amount of suspense and a constant feeling of danger. Especially since the story doesn't have a lot of characters, making those moments much more interesting and rich. Also, bold decisions were made in the pursuit of making the stakes feel high, and I must applaud it.

Spoilers ahead.

However, not everything was perfect, and I think some things could have been handled a lot better, especially the relationship between Scarlett and Tella. You see, throughout the entire book we know that the main goal is to find Tella, who was kidnapped inside Caraval, so Scarlett, her sister, goes above and beyond trying to accomplish that. But it was astonishing the amount of times that the narrator needed to tell us and remind us that she loves her sister, so we could understand her motivations.

I mean, we know that because Tella is Scarlett's sister, she's going to do everything in order to find her, but since Tella is mostly an entity in the entire book, we don't really care about her. I actually think that solving the mystery of her disappearance was the least interesting thing about the book, because she's just severely underdeveloped up to that point. So then, when we get to the end and some reveals are made, I was left wondering like… why is Scarlett just accepting this?

If this was real, I would probably go to the same extremes that Scarlett went for my siblings, but if they did to me what Tella did to Scarlett, man… I would have exploded, and the fact that Scarlett just moved on so easily is a slap in the face, honestly.

Which brings me to the second thing I didn't liked about 'Caraval', but to explain it, I need to acknowledge that I LOVED Julian. I always enjoy male characters in fantasy where they don't get typecast in the typical alpha role where they are the better fighter and the best-looking man to ever walk on Earth who feel the need to protect the female protagonist against everything with their big muscles. It's refreshing to see a mostly typical guy who is an extrovert, and makes jokes, and it's not tied to a trauma from their past.

And because I loved him, I was devastated when he “died” at the book's climax. I was terribly sad, but at the same time I was thoroughly surprised about the guts that the author had in order to do that. It was so refreshing, especially because it seemed so final. And then, the last 15 pages happened.

Don't get me wrong, I mostly liked the ending because it was cute and Julian is my favorite, but I was disappointed that not just Julian was alive, Tella was too (yeah, she pretended to be dead) and Dante was too. Everything that worked so well to make the book feel different and exciting was destroyed in a matter of a few paragraphs. And I know this was probably because of its demographic, but it would have been so satisfying to get a bittersweet ending for once, instead of a fairy tale one.

Of course, I'm still going to read the rest of the series. Despite its faults, I really enjoyed my time with this book, and I'm sure Stephanie Garber has more magic up her sleeve, so we'll see how the rest of the series turns out to be.
description:
Welcome, welcome to CARAVAL, Stephanie Garber’s fantasy debut about two sisters swept up in a mysterious competition filled with magic, heartbreak, and danger.

Scarlett has never left the tiny island where she and her beloved sister, Tella, live with their powerful and cruel father. Now Scarlett’s father has arranged a marriage for her, and Scarlett thinks her dreams of seeing Caraval, the far-away, once-a-year performance where the audience participates in the show, are over.

But this year, Scarlett's long-dreamt-of invitation finally arrives. With the help of a mysterious sailor, Tella whisks Scarlett away to attend. Only, as soon as they arrive, Tella is kidnapped by Caraval’s mastermind organizer, Legend. It turns out that this season's Caraval revolves around Tella, and whoever finds her first is the winner.

Scarlett has been told that everything that happens during Caraval is only an elaborate performance. But whether Caraval is real or not, she must find Tella before the five nights of the game are over, and her sister disappears forever.

title: The Inheritance Games (The Inheritance Games, #1)
author: Jennifer Lynn Barnes
review:
This is a good one!!

Not a life changing book, but not everything you read has to be that way. It was fun, it was intriguing and the mystery was really good.

Maybe the ending was a bit rushed and the “resolution” was a tad simple, but that was meant to happen because it became all so convoluted by the end, that there was no way it could have been really satisfying.

That being said, I’m really excited for the second book because I just want to know more and more about the Hawthorne’s and Avery, especially. I was afraid this was going to be a “not like other girls” situation, but fortunately she was a really cool character that I just want to keep reading about.

4 solid stars, all in all.
description:
Avery Grambs has a plan for a better future: survive high school, win a scholarship, and get out. But her fortunes change in an instant when billionaire Tobias Hawthorne dies and leaves Avery virtually his entire fortune. The catch? Avery has no idea why -- or even who Tobias Hawthorne is.

To receive her inheritance, Avery must move into sprawling, secret passage-filled Hawthorne House, where every room bears the old man's touch -- and his love of puzzles, riddles, and codes. Unfortunately for Avery, Hawthorne House is also occupied by the family that Tobias Hawthorne just dispossessed. This includes the four Hawthorne grandsons: dangerous, magnetic, brilliant boys who grew up with every expectation that one day, they would inherit billions. Heir apparent Grayson Hawthorne is convinced that Avery must be a conwoman, and he's determined to take her down. His brother, Jameson, views her as their grandfather's last hurrah: a twisted riddle, a puzzle to be solved. Caught in a world of wealth and privilege, with danger around every turn, Avery will have to play the game herself just to survive.

title: The Final Girl Support Group
author: Grady Hendrix
review:
The higher you are, the harder you fall, and that's what happened with my expectations for 'The Final Girl Support Group'

It's not that I didn't liked it, it's just that I expected something else...something more. I was promised a horror novel, but it was more of an action thriller type of book, which is fine, but not what I was hoping for.

Now, there were some chilling descriptions and passages in here that were spooky, but not enough to even give me goosebumps, and that's disappointing, because I wanted so much to be scared by it (or at least have fun like in a slasher movie) and in that regard, it failed me.

I think the end was a bit rushed, the motivation behind the murders was, for one of the killers stupid (a watered down version of the motive behind the killer in Scream 4), and for the other incomprehensible. I mean, did we even got a reason for why Skye 'hated' them? It's silly and not in a fun way but a confusing one because of the wasted potential and inconsistencies.

However, not everything was bad. Once I discovered I was in for more of a thrilling ride, especially in the second half of the book, it did got better. The plot was fast-paced and even when the MC was annoying, you understood where she was coming from, so it made sense within the story.

All in all, generally I liked it, it has some fun surprises and Easter eggs along the way for slasher and horror fans, but I didn't loved it, which is a shame because this one looked like a winner at first.
description:
In horror movies, the final girls are the ones left standing when the credits roll. They made it through the worst night of their lives…but what happens after?

From chain saws to summer camp slayers, The Final Girl Support Group pays tribute to and slyly subverts our most popular horror films—movies like The Texas Chainsaw Massacre, A Nightmare on Elm Street, and Scream.

Lynnette Tarkington is a real-life final girl who survived a massacre. For more than a decade, she’s been meeting with five other final girls and their therapist in a support group for those who survived the unthinkable, working to put their lives back together. Then one woman misses a meeting, and their worst fears are realized—someone knows about the group and is determined to rip their lives apart again, piece by piece.

But the thing about final girls is that no matter how bad the odds, how dark the night, how sharp the knife, they will never, ever give up.

title: The Last House on Needless Street
author: Catriona Ward
review:
Wow! What did I just read?

This was easily one of the most confusing and hard to dissect books I've ever read, both for the good and the bad.

Is it horror? I wouldn't call it so. It may have some chilling descriptions, but I was never scared. Especially because I knew that there was *something* deep within the book that would make it all made sense and that prevented it to go full horror. And that was a bit of a humdrum (or at least it was for me) since it doesn't rush to make sense. We have 3 main POVs and 2 secondary ones, and while you may think you know how they connect, the narration makes sure you always doubt about what is happening. And I don't know… it's hard to talk about it without getting spoiler-y, but even when I'm all in for unreliable narrators and confusing storylines, it lacked excitement for the most part. Especially in the first half.

However, once it starts to connect the dots, it definitely gets better. There may not a big GASP moment when it comes to the reveals, but there are so many organic twists and turns that really help to elevate the story and the previously confusing storylines into a cohesive circle that absolutely works. I started frustrated because of the confusion, and ended up with a little heart-wrenching smile on my face, especially when I knew that this story came from an author that really cares about her characters and the issues they (and many real people) face because of childhood abuse, trauma and mental illness.

Now that I think about it, this IS a horror story, but not because of what happens IN the book, but for what it portrays about the real world.
description:
In a boarded-up house on a dead-end street at the edge of the wild Washington woods lives a family of three.

A teenage girl who isn’t allowed outside, not after last time.

A man who drinks alone in front of his TV, trying to ignore the gaps in his memory.

And a house cat who loves napping and reading the Bible.

An unspeakable secret binds them together, but when a new neighbor moves in next door, what is buried out among the birch trees may come back to haunt them all.

title: Finlay Donovan Is Killing It (Finlay Donovan, #1)
author: Elle Cosimano
review:
So, this was fun.

This was a bit out of my confort zone since I'm not usually a fan of comedies, especially mystery comedies, but something about Finlay Donovan just clicked.

The characters were amazing, the story was well-paced and there were some interesting twists I didn't see coming. While I never laughed out loud while reading it, I did chuckled a bit sometimes but it was mostly because of some acute observations by Finlay's part, or a funny dialogue, not because of the situations she was in. Probably that was what the author intended, or maybe not, but I still had a good time with this one, and I'm ready for the sequel. That cliffhanger was so good to resist the next one.
description:
"Getting the job done" for one single mom takes on a whole new meaning in Finlay Donovan is Killing It.

Finlay Donovan is killing it . . . except, she’s really not. She’s a stressed-out single-mom of two and struggling novelist, Finlay’s life is in chaos: the new book she promised her literary agent isn’t written, her ex-husband fired the nanny without telling her, and this morning she had to send her four-year-old to school with hair duct-taped to her head after an incident with scissors.

When Finlay is overheard discussing the plot of her new suspense novel with her agent over lunch, she’s mistaken for a contract killer, and inadvertently accepts an offer to dispose of a problem husband in order to make ends meet . . . Soon, Finlay discovers that crime in real life is a lot more difficult than its fictional counterpart, as she becomes tangled in a real-life murder investigation.

Fast-paced, deliciously witty, and wholeheartedly authentic in depicting the frustrations and triumphs of motherhood in all its messiness, hilarity, and heartfelt moment, Finlay Donovan Is Killing It is the first in a brilliant new series from YA Edgar Award nominee Elle Cosimano.

title: The Push
author: Ashley Audrain
review:
WOW, I don’t remember the last time I read a whole book in just a day and a half.

This book was, up to a certain point, what I expected it to be, but also nothing like it.

When I read a bit about it online I was like: ‘oh, it’s just a ‘We Need to Talk About Kevin’ rip-off’ and my mind was blown away when I realized that even thought they do have some points in common, this is a completely different beast.

A fresh mix between a domestic thriller, a drama and even horror at some points, ‘The Push’ is like nothing I’ve ever read before and I can’t rate it anything lower than 5 stars.

I can’t say much more without spoiling, so I’ll keep it short, but easily on my top 3 of books this year!
description:
An alternative cover edition for this ISBN can be found here.

A tense, page-turning psychological drama about the making and breaking of a family–and a woman whose experience of motherhood is nothing at all what she hoped for–and everything she feared.

Blythe Connor is determined that she will be the warm, comforting mother to her new baby Violet that she herself never had.

But in the thick of motherhood’s exhausting early days, Blythe becomes convinced that something is wrong with her daughter–she doesn’t behave like most children do.

Or is it all in Blythe’s head? Her husband, Fox, says she’s imagining things. The more Fox dismisses her fears, the more Blythe begins to question her own sanity, and the more we begin to question what Blythe is telling us about her life as well.

Then their son Sam is born–and with him, Blythe has the blissful connection she’d always imagined with her child. Even Violet seems to love her little brother. But when life as they know it is changed in an instant, the devastating fall-out forces Blythe to face the truth.

The Push is a tour de force you will read in a sitting, an utterly immersive novel that will challenge everything you think you know about motherhood, about what we owe our children, and what it feels like when women are not believed.

title: House of Hollow
author: Krystal Sutherland
review:
This is a 3 stars read to me, and I’m conflicted by it.

The first half of the book was AMAZING, I really mean it. The mystery was exciting, the writing was beautiful and the characters, if not lovable, at least were intriguing. I could sense some wrongness in the situation the sisters were living in, and it was so refreshing. I was ready for a 5 star read.

And then the second half of the book came and it all went downhill. Just by the 50% mark of the book, something happens that makes the whole mysterious vibe crash down and it never really gets back on track. Suddenly it becomes a Riverdale meets Alice in Wonderland type of story that not even reaches the level of ridiculousness the former has, or well… the wonder from the latter.

Finally, I thought that the *twist* might have been worthy, but it just wasn’t, really. It’s not a bad twist, but it’s kind of a predictable one (in the context of this story in particular), so I can’t even say that my mind was blown away by the end.

All in all, I think my main feeling is disappointment because of the wasted potential and the enormous letdown the second half of the book brings, especially after those amazing first 140 pages.
description:
Seventeen-year-old Iris Hollow has always been strange. Something happened to her and her two older sisters when they were children, something they can’t quite remember but that left each of them with an identical half-moon scar at the base of their throats.

Iris has spent most of her teenage years trying to avoid the weirdness that sticks to her like tar. But when her eldest sister, Grey, goes missing under suspicious circumstances, Iris learns just how weird her life can get: horned men start shadowing her, a corpse falls out of her sister’s ceiling, and ugly, impossible memories start to twist their way to the forefront of her mind.

As Iris retraces Grey’s last known footsteps and follows the increasingly bizarre trail of breadcrumbs she left behind, it becomes apparent that the only way to save her sister is to decipher the mystery of what happened to them as children.

The closer Iris gets to the truth, the closer she comes to understanding that the answer is dark and dangerous – and that Grey has been keeping a terrible secret from her for years.

title: Firekeeper’s Daughter (Firekeeper's Daughter, #1)
author: Angeline Boulley
review:
I know this is going to be an unpopular opinion, but I don't know why people LOVE this book.

I don't know, I think this is my 'Where the Crawdads Sing' situation of 2022 where a book is so hyped that it doesn't meet my expectations, or it's probably just not my genre.

But why wouldn't it be? It's YA and I really like the genre, also it's sold as a thriller, which I also tend to love, but I didn't click with it, and I think that was because of 4 main reasons:

1. This may be most of a personal reason, but a big part of the plot revolves around hockey. And not just by making quick references or some vague mentions, hockey breathes through the novel and there are chapters where hockey matches are played with so much detail that I can just tell that the author is a fan. FYI, apart from being a YA semi-mystery, this could also be read as a sports novel. And for me, that's a no-no.

2. The main characters, unfortunately, don't feel like much like characters. On one side, we have our main girl Daunis who tends to feel like an info-dumper most of the time, especially during the first third. I know this is a debut and given the context and background of her character, this was probably needed, but 90 pages of pure background information before anything happens, is just too much. On the other hand, Jamie… I won't say much, but for just one second did we really believed he could be an FBI agent? C'mon… he’s the most useless FBI agent I’ve ever read about.

3. Apart from them (and probably Levi and Auntie Teddy), any other character was, curiously, over mentioned, but at the same time underdeveloped. I don't know how to explain it, but I don't think that many characters were necessary. Especially since many of them were around for a few chapters, and then you just had to remember what they did for everything to make sense at the end. Maybe it was just me, since I was mostly skim reading past the 150-page mark, but it was hard to keep up sometimes.

4. The thrill factor. Also, probably not the book's fault, but when something is sold as a thriller, I expect to be… well, thrilled. This didn't happen, except during the climax. The rest of if was mostly a mystery, which was fine, but for me, it was too slow. It didn't need to be a 500 pages book.

Now, was it all terrible? Nope. There were some things I liked, but I would like to highlight two things:

1. The ending was so powerful. And I'm not talking about the revelations of the mystery, per se (which were also good… a bit unbelievable, but good) but a thing that happened in the last 100 pages and that, unfortunately, didn't have a lot of consequences for the perpetrator. I won't say what it is, but if you've read it, you know, and even if I think these type of creative decision may be hard to take and even judged by some, I think that what Angeline Boulley did with that storyline was the saddest thing to happen in the whole book, but also was so believable, that glossing over it or not giving it the weight it deserves, would have been a disservice to any young woman who reads it.

2. Here comes a spoiler, but I was so glad to see that Daunis didn't stay with Jamie, at least for now. Everything in their relationship was a lie (even if their love wasn't) and they both needed to grow, breathe and figure out their feelings before committing to being together officially. That was a mature decision and I applaud it.

All in all, this wasn't my favorite book and I would recommend it mostly because it is important to have different cultures in literature and this one does the job, I just wished I liked the story and characters better than I did.
description:
As a biracial, unenrolled tribal member and the product of a scandal, Daunis Fontaine has never quite fit in—both in her hometown and on the nearby Ojibwe reservation. When her family is struck by tragedy, Daunis puts her dreams on hold to care for her fragile mother. The only bright spot is meeting Jamie, the charming new recruit on her brother’s hockey team.

After Daunis witnesses a shocking murder that thrusts her into a criminal investigation, she agrees to go undercover. But the deceptions—and deaths—keep piling up and soon the threat strikes too close to home. How far will she go to protect her community if it means tearing apart the only world she’s ever known?

title: Clockwork Princess (The Infernal Devices, #3)
author: Cassandra Clare
review:
Wow, that epilogue!

Truth be told, I wasn't feeling this book during the first third, but it did turn around. Why I wasn't a fan? Mostly because I didn't care at all about the plot. I know we needed to get through that, but I was here just for the characters.

I refuse to believe that the same woman who created the worst romantic relationship ever (Jace and Clary) could also write the only love triangle I've loved in any book I've ever read. That is something amazing. But it's true.

The relationship between Will, Jem, and Tessa was the glue that holds this entire series together and I'm glad to, at last, finish it, so I can read about why people love and still talk about "The Infernal Devices" without spoiling myself.

Was it all too easy? Yes. Did I care? No. Maybe we didn't need 100 pages to finally end the trilogy, but the epilogue was something else and made up for any faults the book could have.

I won't add much (everybody already read this one). I just loved it.
description:
A net of shadows begins to tighten around the Shadowhunters of the London Institute. Mortmain plans to use his Infernal Devices, an army of pitiless automatons, to destroy the Shadowhunters. He needs only one last item to complete his plan: he needs Tessa Gray.

Charlotte Branwell, head of the London Institute, is desperate to find Mortmain before he strikes. But when Mortmain abducts Tessa, the boys who lay equal claim to her heart, Jem and Will, will do anything to save her. For though Tessa and Jem are now engaged, Will is as much in love with her as ever.

As those who love Tessa rally to rescue her from Mortmain’s clutches, Tessa realizes that the only person who can save her is herself. But can a single girl, even one who can command the power of angels, face down an entire army?

Danger and betrayal, secrets and enchantment, and the tangled threads of love and loss intertwine as the Shadowhunters are pushed to the very brink of destruction in the breathtaking conclusion to the Infernal Devices trilogy.

title: City of Heavenly Fire (The Mortal Instruments, #6)
author: Cassandra Clare
review:
A great way to finish this whole saga.
It almost redeemed the whole second half of the series.

Also, Tessa and Jem 🥲
description:
Shadowhunters and demons square off for the final showdown in the spellbinding, seductive conclusion to the #1 New York Times bestselling Mortal Instruments series.

Darkness has descended on the Shadowhunter world. Chaos and destruction overwhelm the Nephilim as Clary, Jace, Simon, and their friends band together to fight the greatest evil they have ever faced: Clary’s own brother. Sebastian Morgenstern is on the move, systematically turning Shadowhunter against Shadowhunter. Bearing the Infernal Cup, he transforms Shadowhunters into creatures of nightmare, tearing apart families and lovers as the ranks of his Endarkened army swell. Nothing in this world can defeat Sebastian—but if they journey to the realm of demons, they just might have a chance…

Lives will be lost, love sacrificed, and the whole world will change. Who will survive the explosive sixth and final installment of the Mortal Instruments series?

title: City of Lost Souls (The Mortal Instruments, #5)
author: Cassandra Clare
review:
I don't know how much I can add about an old sequel from a very old YA series, so I think I'll keep this one short.

It definitely is a step-up from the previous book, which was mostly terrible and boring, but I still can't remember half of what happens here besides "Jace is evil and horny now... and now he's not". I had fun, it was a pleasant read, and, for the first time, the relationship between Clary and Jace was not an eye-rolling one, even if she is still one of the most stupid main characters I've ever read.

Definitely, one of the best decisions Cassandra Clare made regarding this book was finally giving other characters a time in the spotlight with the constantly changing POV. It turned the book into a more dynamic read, even if sometimes nothing was really happening.

However, it doesn't hold up as well as the original trilogy since everything feels like an afterthought (which we all know that it was). And a long one at that.
description:
What price is too high to pay, even for love? Plunge into fifth installment in the internationally bestselling Mortal Instruments series and “prepare to be hooked” (Entertainment Weekly)—now with a gorgeous new cover, a map, a new foreword, and exclusive bonus content! City of Lost Souls is a Shadowhunters novel.

When Jace and Clary meet again, Clary is horrified to discover that the demon Lilith’s magic has bound her beloved Jace together with her evil brother Sebastian, and that Jace has become a servant of evil. The Clave is out to destroy Sebastian, but there is no way to harm one boy without destroying the other. As Alec, Magnus, Simon, and Isabelle wheedle and bargain with Seelies, demons, and the merciless Iron Sisters to try to save Jace, Clary plays a dangerous game of her own. The price of losing is not just her own life, but Jace’s soul. She’s willing to do anything for Jace, but can she still trust him? Or is he truly lost?

Love. Blood. Betrayal. Revenge. Darkness threatens to claim the Shadowhunters in the harrowing fifth book of the Mortal Instruments series.

title: City of Fallen Angels (The Mortal Instruments, #4)
author: Cassandra Clare
review:
Oh well, not everything can be perfect.

I knew beforehand that this was the least liked TMI book in the whole series, but I didn't knew how bad it could get. Admittedly, for almost three quarters of the book, this was a 2 star read: the characters were annoying, the plot was dragged on and on and on, the romantic subplots were stupid and it was just soooo boring. Literally nothing was happening, Clary & Co just moved from one place to another doing absolutely nothing.

I seriously started to wonder if I was going to be able to read the second half of this series... and hopefully the last 150 pages really turned this book around and became what the rest of these books used to be: fun, exciting and while silly, very entertaining. Yes, the 'who' in this terrible whodunnit was underwhelming, but the idea behind the twist was good. I seriously believe that the author had some good ideas for this book (and probably the fifth and sixth book will be better) but they were executed in the worst way possible by making the whole set of characters just plainly unlikeable until the very end when they just discovered the magic of communicating (except for Clary and Jace... they just refuse to grow up).

Like I said, if if wasn't for the last 150 pages, the fact that we got to know Isabelle a whole lot more than on previous books, and that it has a killer cliffhanger, this would be a 2 star read, however, just because of those things I decided to bump it up to 3 stars. I seriously hope that this was a misstep and we can go back to the excitement the rest of these books brought me in the past.

Edit: I re-rated it to 2 stars, it was bad.
description:
The Mortal War is over, and sixteen-year-old Clary Fray is back home in New York, excited about all the possibilities before her. She’s training to become a Shadowhunter and to use her unique power. Her mother is getting married to the love of her life. Downworlders and Shadowhunters are at peace at last. And—most importantly of all—she can finally call Jace her boyfriend.

But nothing comes without a price.

Someone is murdering Shadowhunters, provoking tensions between Downworlders and Shadowhunters that could lead to a second, bloody war. Clary’s best friend, Simon, can’t help her—his mother just found out that he’s a vampire, and now he’s homeless. When Jace begins to pull away from her without explaining why, Clary is forced to delve into the heart of a mystery whose solution reveals her worst she herself has set in motion a terrible chain of events that could lead to her losing everything she loves. Even Jace.

title: Clockwork Prince (The Infernal Devices, #2)
author: Cassandra Clare
review:
It’s definitely not as good as the first one, since the whole book doesn’t have much of a plot and we’re still on the same situation as we were at the end of the first one regarding Mortmain and his automatons and stuff, but it’s as addictive as the previous one, especially during the second half of the book, and you become SO invested in the romance that’s it’s hard to look away. I am not the biggest fan of love triangles, but here we can find an amazingly written one.

Now I see why many people prefer this series over TMI, and I totally agree. Even if there’s not much happening, the characters are worth a read.
description:
In the magical underworld of Victorian London, Tessa Gray has at last found safety with the Shadowhunters. But that safety proves fleeting when rogue forces in the Clave plot to see her protector, Charlotte, replaced as head of the Institute. If Charlotte loses her position, Tessa will be out on the street—and easy prey for the mysterious Magister, who wants to use Tessa’s powers for his own dark ends.

With the help of the handsome, self-destructive Will and the fiercely devoted Jem, Tessa discovers that the Magister’s war on the Shadowhunters is deeply personal. He blames them for a long-ago tragedy that shattered his life. To unravel the secrets of the past, the trio journeys from mist-shrouded Yorkshire to a manor house that holds untold horrors, from the slums of London to an enchanted ballroom where Tessa discovers that the truth of her parentage is more sinister than she had imagined. When they encounter a clockwork demon bearing a warning for Will, they realize that the Magister himself knows their every move—and that one of their own has betrayed them.

Tessa finds her heart drawn more and more to Jem, but her longing for Will, despite his dark moods, continues to unsettle her. But something is changing in Will—the wall he has built around himself is crumbling. Could finding the Magister free Will from his secrets and give Tessa the answers about who she is and what she was born to do?

As their dangerous search for the Magister and the truth leads the friends into peril, Tessa learns that when love and lies are mixed, they can corrupt even the purest heart.

title: Clockwork Angel (The Infernal Devices, #1)
author: Cassandra Clare
review: This was simply amazing from start to finish!
description:
Magic is dangerous—but love is more dangerous still.

When sixteen-year-old Tessa Gray crosses the ocean to find her brother, her destination is England, the time is the reign of Queen Victoria, and something terrifying is waiting for her in London’s Downworld, where vampires, warlocks, and other supernatural folk stalk the gaslit streets. Only the Shadowhunters, warriors dedicated to ridding the world of demons, keep order amidst the chaos.

Kidnapped by the mysterious Dark Sisters, members of a secret organization called The Pandemonium Club, Tessa soon learns that she herself is a Downworlder with a rare ability: the power to transform, at will, into another person. What’s more, the Magister, the shadowy figure who runs the Club, will stop at nothing to claim Tessa’s power for his own.

Friendless and hunted, Tessa takes refuge with the Shadowhunters of the London Institute, who swear to find her brother if she will use her power to help them. She soon finds herself fascinated by—and torn between—two best friends: James, whose fragile beauty hides a deadly secret, and blue-eyed Will, whose caustic wit and volatile moods keep everyone in his life at arm’s length… everyone, that is, but Tessa.

As their search draws them deep into the heart of an arcane plot that threatens to destroy the Shadowhunters, Tessa realizes that she may need to choose between saving her brother and helping her new friends save the world… and that love may be the most dangerous magic of all.

title: City of Glass (The Mortal Instruments, #3)
author: Cassandra Clare
review:
4.5 stars because I just looooove these books!!!

The dialogue can be cheesy, the characters are a bit annoying sometimes, the incest storyline was extended waaaaaay too much, and the villain may have the most stupid motive I’ve ever read, BUT, these are so much fun, and I had a great time reading it.

I’m ready for what’s next
description:
To save her mother’s life, Clary must travel to the City of Glass, the ancestral home of the Shadowhunters—never mind that entering the city without permission is against the Law, and breaking the Law could mean death. To make things worse, she learns that Jace does not want her there, and Simon has been thrown in prison by the Shadowhunters, who are deeply suspicious of a vampire who can withstand sunlight.

As Clary uncovers more about her family’s past, she finds an ally in mysterious Shadowhunter Sebastian. With Valentine mustering the full force of his power to destroy all Shadowhunters forever, their only chance to defeat him is to fight alongside their eternal enemies. But can Downworlders and Shadowhunters put aside their hatred to work together? While Jace realizes exactly how much he’s willing to risk for Clary, can she harness her newfound powers to help save the Glass City—whatever the cost?

title: City of Ashes (The Mortal Instruments, #2)
author: Cassandra Clare
review:
Even if I was annoyed by the whole “Simon is dying/dead/going to die” thing that happens not once, not twice but THREE times in this book, I was obsessed with it and I couldn’t stop reading!

I lovedddd it, there’s nothing more I can say
description:
Clary Fray just wishes that her life would go back to normal. But what’s normal when you’re a demon-slaying Shadowhunter, your mother is in a magically induced coma, and you can suddenly see Downworlders like werewolves, vampires, and faeries? If Clary left the world of the Shadowhunters behind, it would mean more time with her best friend, Simon, who’s becoming more than a friend. But the Shadowhunting world isn’t ready to let her go—especially her handsome, infuriating, newfound brother, Jace. And Clary’s only chance to help her mother is to track down rogue Shadowhunter Valentine, who is probably insane, certainly evil—and also her father.

To complicate matters, someone in New York City is murdering Downworlder children. Is Valentine behind the killings—and if he is, what is he trying to do? When the second of the Mortal Instruments, the Soul-Sword, is stolen, the terrifying Inquisitor arrives to investigate and zooms right in on Jace. How can Clary stop Valentine if Jace is willing to betray everything he believes in to help their father?

In this breathtaking sequel to City of Bones, Cassandra Clare lures her readers back into the dark grip of New York City’s Downworld, where love is never safe and power becomes the deadliest temptation.

title: Cinder (The Lunar Chronicles, #1)
author: Marissa Meyer
review: Fun but a tad predictable!
description:
The prince straightened, forcing her gaze to follow him. “You’re not quite what I was expecting.”

Humans and androids crowd the raucous streets of New Beijing. A deadly plague ravages the population. From space, a ruthless lunar people watch, waiting to make their move. No one knows that Earth's fate hinges on one girl. . . .

Cinder, a gifted mechanic, is a cyborg. She's a second-class citizen with a mysterious past, reviled by her stepmother and blamed for her stepsister's illness. But when her life becomes intertwined with the handsome Prince Kai's, she suddenly finds herself at the center of an intergalactic struggle, and a forbidden attraction. Caught between duty and freedom, loyalty and betrayal, she must uncover secrets about her past in order to protect her world's future.

With high-stakes action and a smart, resourceful heroine, Cinder is a Cinderella retelling that is at once classic and strikingly original.

title: Legendborn (The Legendborn Cycle, #1)
author: Tracy Deonn
review:
So, this one was good. Really good… 4.5 stars good.

Now, I won't deny that I was a bit intimidated by this book because it's the first one in a series, it is long and the font is a bit small, but when you have a good story in your hands, nothing else matters. You're glued to the pages, and they just fly by.

I really don't know what to say about it because I would really advise to anyone who goes into it, to just go blind. Yes, it is a bit of a retelling of the Arthurian legends, but it is also SO much more. It has incredible depth (at least with our MC), the story takes her Blackness and her heritage to really propel how the plot progresses, it has some amazing representation, and it's just intriguing to see how it all develops before your eyes.

Is it perfect? I don't think so: the world building is ENORMOUS and confusing. By the end of it, I kind of grasped the most important things about it, but some other things I just plainly ignored because there were a lot of names and ranks to remember that they all blurred together. And that leads me to another point that acts to the detriment of the overall story: it has so many characters that you can't keep up with them.

Don't get me wrong: I can manage a lot of characters. Many books have this big cast of characters to get to know and remember, but it's not just remembering them, it's getting to know them, and that's where 'Legendborn' fails a bit. We do get to know Bree, Nick, Sel, Alice, and a couple of others, but we also have like 7 more secondary characters who just pop up out of nowhere and who are actually important to the story, and we do not know anything about them besides their name. This not only leads to apathy towards them and for the reader to get frustrated and ignore their existence, but it also diminishes the impact some events (especially in the last third of the book) should have.

I read some reviews about this book that say it is a predictable YA adventure, but I mostly disagree. Yes, it definitely has some clichés of the genre like a love triangle, the moody with a haunting secret male character who we all hate in the beginning, but then we grow to care about, the chosen-one journey, the betrayal at the end by someone we thought was an ally and so on, but it also brings so much more to its story by treating topics like race, gender, sexuality and cultural heritage that you can rarely find in YA. And just because of that, I think it's worth a read.

Besides, it is really exciting. Just read it.
description:
An Instant New York Times Bestseller!
Winner of the Coretta Scott King - John Steptoe for New Talent Author Award

Filled with mystery and an intriguingly rich magic system, Tracy Deonn's YA contemporary fantasy Legendborn offers the dark allure of City of Bones with a modern-day twist on a classic legend and a lot of Southern Black Girl Magic.

After her mother dies in an accident, sixteen-year-old Bree Matthews wants nothing to do with her family memories or childhood home. A residential program for bright high schoolers at UNC-Chapel Hill seems like the perfect escape — until Bree witnesses a magical attack her very first night on campus.

A flying demon feeding on human energies.

A secret society of so called "Legendborn" students that hunt the creatures down.

And a mysterious teenage mage who calls himself a "Merlin" and who attempts — and fails — to wipe Bree's memory of everything she saw.

The mage's failure unlocks Bree's own unique magic and a buried memory with a hidden connection: the night her mother died, another Merlin was at the hospital. Now that Bree knows there's more to her mother's death than what's on the police report, she'll do whatever it takes to find out the truth, even if that means infiltrating the Legendborn as one of their initiates.

She recruits Nick, a self-exiled Legendborn with his own grudge against the group, and their reluctant partnership pulls them deeper into the society's secrets — and closer to each other. But when the Legendborn reveal themselves as the descendants of King Arthur's knights and explain that a magical war is coming, Bree has to decide how far she'll go for the truth and whether she should use her magic to take the society down — or join the fight.

title: The Empire of Gold (The Daevabad Trilogy, #3)
author: S.A. Chakraborty
review:
Wow, this was a long and wild book

I don’t know if there is much to say about a third and final book in a fantasy trilogy, so I’ll try to keep it short.

These were good, without ever being my favorite. The Daevabad books were, from the start, so much more complex than the usual fantasy series tend to be, and while I can appreciate that, it’s also the thing that makes me NOT love it. It was, at the end, too convoluted and complicated for my taste, and I was just like “oh, ok, here’s ANOTHER complicated past secret/heritage/pact to have in mind”, and while this can be fun, too much of it is tedious, and I think, at the end, it was an overused element.

Just like in previous books, the author really excels much more in the more intimate and character driven moments than in the plot ones, because of the same reasons I just mentioned, which ultimately makes The Empire of Gold fall behind the second book (my favorite in the trilogy, tbh), because this one has the task to close every storyline, and since Chakraborty was already in a politically charged and convoluted plot, there was no easy way out. I can applaud that complexity in a novel, and a lot of people may like it, but I just got lost by the end.

However I ultimately fell in love with the characters and how they always stay true to their original selfs since the first book, and if I stayed reading this series for more than 2000 pages is because, despite its many faults, you can’t help but care about what is going on with its charismatic characters.

Taking the three books in consideration, I think the whole trilogy is a solid 4 star read to me, and I’m excited for the books Chakraborty will bring in the future.
description:
The final chapter in the Daevabad Trilogy, in which a con-woman and an idealistic djinn prince join forces to save a magical kingdom from a devastating civil war.

Daevabad has fallen.

After a brutal conquest stripped the city of its magic, Nahid leader Banu Manizheh and her resurrected commander, Dara, must try to repair their fraying alliance and stabilize a fractious, warring people.

But the bloodletting and loss of his beloved Nahri have unleashed the worst demons of Dara’s dark past. To vanquish them, he must face some ugly truths about his history and put himself at the mercy of those he once considered enemies.

Having narrowly escaped their murderous families and Daevabad’s deadly politics, Nahri and Ali, now safe in Cairo, face difficult choices of their own. While Nahri finds peace in the old rhythms and familiar comforts of her human home, she is haunted by the knowledge that the loved ones she left behind and the people who considered her a savior are at the mercy of a new tyrant. Ali, too, cannot help but look back, and is determined to return to rescue his city and the family that remains. Seeking support in his mother’s homeland, he discovers that his connection to the marid goes far deeper than expected and threatens not only his relationship with Nahri, but his very faith.

As peace grows more elusive and old players return, Nahri, Ali, and Dara come to understand that in order to remake the world, they may need to fight those they once loved . . . and take a stand for those they once hurt.

title: The Kingdom of Copper (The Daevabad Trilogy, #2)
author: S.A. Chakraborty
review:
OMG with those last 5 chapters, they were one of the most engrossing pages I've ever read.

I feel a little bad for the 4-star rating because this is actually a 4.5 read, but something in me doesn't feel like it should be upped to a 5, mainly because I think it's a bit longer that it should and the middle dragged a bit in consequence.

However, I felt more engrossed on this book than I was on the first one, probably because the whole tribe situation is so much easier to follow, the 3 POVs were interesting and weren't all that disconnected, even though 1 one of them was for the 90% of the book and interesting developments were scattered throughout the whole book, instead of just on the last couple of chapters.

I think that actually this book made me realize that my actual rating to the first one is a 3.5, not a 4, because I was a reluctant to start 'The Kingdom of Copper' and now I'm definitely eager to start 'The Empire of Gold'

Btw, I don't know why but on the first one I really liked Dara, and now he irritates me... he's just so useless and just follows directions even though he knows what he is doing is wrong. Anyway, let's see how this ends...
description:
Return to Daevabad in the spellbinding sequel to THE CITY OF BRASS.

Nahri’s life changed forever the moment she accidentally summoned Dara, a formidable, mysterious djinn, during one of her schemes. Whisked from her home in Cairo, she was thrust into the dazzling royal court of Daevabad and quickly discovered she would need all her grifter instincts to survive there.

Now, with Daevabad entrenched in the dark aftermath of the battle that saw Dara slain at Prince Ali’s hand, Nahri must forge a new path for herself, without the protection of the guardian who stole her heart or the counsel of the prince she considered a friend. But even as she embraces her heritage and the power it holds, she knows she’s been trapped in a gilded cage, watched by a king who rules from the throne that once belonged to her familyand one misstep will doom her tribe.

Meanwhile, Ali has been exiled for daring to defy his father. Hunted by assassins, adrift on the unforgiving copper sands of his ancestral land, he is forced to rely on the frightening abilities the marid, the unpredictable water spirits, have gifted him. But in doing so, he threatens to unearth a terrible secret his family has long kept buried.

And as a new century approaches and the djinn gather within Daevabad's towering brass walls for celebrations, a threat brews unseen in the desolate north. It’s a force that would bring a storm of fire straight to the city’s gates . . . and one that seeks the aid of a warrior trapped between worlds, torn between a violent duty he can never escape and a peace he fears he will never deserve.

title: Serpent & Dove (Serpent & Dove, #1)
author: Shelby Mahurin
review:
What an amazing 4.5 star read ‘Serpent & Dove’ was.

It was romantic, exciting and while a bit overlong (the first 1/3 was a bit lacking) the rest of the book really made up for it. Now, I must admit that the plot it’s not the most innovative or groundbreaking, but a handful of well written characters and a well constructed romance were just what it needed.

Not everything was perfect, especially like I said in the first 150 pages or so. The author took her time to really establish the world and the situation in hand, and sometimes it was done a little bit sloppily, but since this book is a debut I must applaud the addictiveness and great pacing of the story that Mahurin also imprinted in here.

I don’t have too much to add, I’m nervous about the second book since I know it’s not a beloved one, but I’ll make sure to read it soon.
description:
Bound as one to love, honor, or burn.

Two years ago, Louise le Blanc fled her coven and took shelter in the city of Cesarine, forsaking all magic and living off whatever she could steal. There, witches like Lou are hunted. They are feared. And they are burned.

Sworn to the Church as a Chasseur, Reid Diggory has lived his life by one principle: thou shalt not suffer a witch to live. His path was never meant to cross with Lou's, but a wicked stunt forces them into an impossible union—holy matrimony.

The war between witches and Church is an ancient one, and Lou's most dangerous enemies bring a fate worse than fire. Unable to ignore her growing feelings, yet powerless to change what she is, a choice must be made.

And love makes fools of us all.

This is a previously published edition of ISBN 9780062878021. An alternate cover edition can be found here.

title: A ​Court of Silver Flames (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #5)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
A bit overlong, but Nesta is now my favorite character in this entire series!

Also, Cassian>>>>Rhys
description:
Sarah J. Maas's sexy, richly imagined series continues with the journey of Feyre's fiery sister, Nesta.

Nesta Archeron has always been prickly-proud, swift to anger, and slow to forgive. And ever since being forced into the Cauldron and becoming High Fae against her will, she's struggled to find a place for herself within the strange, deadly world she inhabits. Worse, she can't seem to move past the horrors of the war with Hybern and all she lost in it.

The one person who ignites her temper more than any other is Cassian, the battle-scarred warrior whose position in Rhysand and Feyre's Night Court keeps him constantly in Nesta's orbit. But her temper isn't the only thing Cassian ignites. The fire between them is undeniable, and only burns hotter as they are forced into close quarters with each other.

Meanwhile, the treacherous human queens who returned to the Continent during the last war have forged a dangerous new alliance, threatening the fragile peace that has settled over the realms. And the key to halting them might very well rely on Cassian and Nesta facing their haunting pasts.

Against the sweeping backdrop of a world seared by war and plagued with uncertainty, Nesta and Cassian battle monsters from within and without as they search for acceptance-and healing-in each other's arms.

title: A Court of Frost and Starlight (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #4)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review: I didn’t care about anything that happened in here, but I want to read the next one, and I’m a purist… 🤷🏻‍♂️
description:
In this companion tale to the bestselling A Court of Thorns and Roses series, Feyre, Rhys and their friends are working to rebuild the Night Court and the vastly changed world beyond after the events of A Court of Wings and Ruin.

But Winter Solstice is finally near, and with it a hard-earned reprieve. Yet even the festive atmosphere can't keep the shadows of the past from looming. As Feyre navigates her first Winter Solstice as High Lady, she finds that those dearest to her have more wounds than she anticipated – scars that will have a far-reaching impact on the future of their court.

title: A Court of Mist and Fury (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #2)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
I’ve done it! I read one of the most beloved SJM’s books and… it wasn’t my favorite.

I mean, I liked it. It’s definitely superior to the first one and there is SO much growth in Feyre, that it amazes me how much I ended up liking her here, when at least for me, she was a weak spot in ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’, but I’m still not head over heels with this series in general, and I can’t really pinpoint why.

Perhaps because they suffer from being overlong and over complicated. I mean, the main story is really basic, but it brings so many subplots and so many little complications along the way, that at one point I was like: c’mon, let’s go back to what we’re really here for, the damn cauldron and the book.

And maybe her other series are not profound or anything, they’re also romantic fantasy, but the fact that we have different POVs in those, and in here it’s only Feyre, I think makes up for a less dynamic reading experience. Also, c’mon, the villains are all caricatures, so the whole climax was not as exciting or exhilarating as it should have been.

I’ll keep reading it, of course. Every Sarah J. Maas book brings so much fun, but out of all the 3 series in her name, I think this one is at the bottom for me.
description:
The seductive and stunning #1 New York Times bestselling sequel to Sarah J. Maas's spellbinding A Court of Thorns and Roses .

Feyre has undergone more trials than one human woman can carry in her heart. Though she's now been granted the powers and lifespan of the High Fae, she is haunted by her time Under the Mountain and the terrible deeds she performed to save the lives of Tamlin and his people.

As her marriage to Tamlin approaches, Feyre's hollowness and nightmares consume her. She finds herself split into two different one who upholds her bargain with Rhysand, High Lord of the feared Night Court, and one who lives out her life in the Spring Court with Tamlin. While Feyre navigates a dark web of politics, passion, and dazzling power, a greater evil looms. She might just be the key to stopping it, but only if she can harness her harrowing gifts, heal her fractured soul, and decide how she wishes to shape her future-and the future of a world in turmoil.

Bestselling author Sarah J. Maas's masterful storytelling brings this second book in her dazzling, sexy, action-packed series to new heights.

title: The Assassin's Blade (Throne of Glass, #0.1-#0.5)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
4.5 stars actually because it started kind of slow, but by the end I was totally in love with this one.

I’m loving this whole series and everyone says they get even better, so here’s to more Celaena!
description:
Discover where Celaena Sardothien's thrilling saga began.

Celaena Sardothien is her kingdom's most feared assassin. Though she works for the powerful and ruthless Assassin's Guild, Celaena yields to no-one and trusts only her fellow killer-for-hire, Sam.

When Celaena's scheming master, Arobynn Hamel, dispatches her on missions that take her from remote islands to hostile deserts, she finds herself acting independently of his wishes—and questioning her own allegiance. Along the way, she makes friends and enemies alike, and discovers that she feels far more for Sam than just friendship. But by defying Arobynn's orders, Celaena risks unimaginable punishment, and with Sam by her side, he is in danger, too. They will have to risk it all if they hope to escape Arobynn's clutches—and if they fail, they'll lose not just a chance at freedom, but their lives...

A prequel to Throne of Glass, this collection of five novellas offers listeners a deeper look into the history of this cunning assassin and her enthralling—and deadly—world.

Included in this volume:

The Assassin and the Pirate Lord
The Assassin and the Healer
The Assassin and the Desert
The Assassin and the Underworld
The Assassin and the Empire

title: Kingdom of Ash (Throne of Glass, #7)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
5 amazing stars!

I can't believe I just finished this series. It has been a journey and I'm really glad that I looked beyond the ugly covers (I'm sorry but I never liked them) to discover how great these books are.

I was a bit nervous at the beginning of 'Kingdom of Ash' because I wasn't sure how Maas was going to be able to wrap everything up. And yes, there were a few cop-outs and some deus ex machina scattered here and there, but for the most part she respected the rules of her own world and played with them to finish the series. We had some unexpected but rewarding developments in here that are appreciated because not everything ended up happening as I was expecting and that is something good.

However, and this might be controversial but I was hoping for a different ending. I liked it, I'm not saying I didn't, and I get that, at the end of the day, this whole thing was kind of a fairy tale... with wars, possessions, assassinations and sex, but a fairy tale nonetheless, but it was just too clean. Too perfect to be real after everything that happened. I mean, it was a BIG war and not even a single MC character died. Of course, a few SC did but they weren't THAT important in the big scheme of things. I always liked the idea that I never knew what was going to happen when it came to the final 200 pages in the Throne of Glass books, but in here there were no real surprises in that aspect.

I respect what Maas did with the story, it was a complicated and convoluted one and props for her because this was a hell of an ending but there were no real shocks and it felt a bit repetitive when it came to the battle scenes (I think a lot of these could have been condensed into one or two big battles because they became kinda tiresome after a bit)

All in all, nothing takes away the big fun I had while reading 'Kingdom of Ash' and almost every book in the series. It was a big ride and I'll probably think about these characters for a long time after today... I just hope that I discover another series that makes me feel like I did when I read this one.

Cheers to Elide for being awesome throughout the whole series without half of the recognition other characters like Aelin or Manon always get, btw.
description:
Aelin Galathynius has vowed to save her people ― but at a tremendous cost. Locked within an iron coffin by the Queen of the Fae, Aelin must draw upon her fiery will as she endures months of torture. The knowledge that yielding to Maeve will doom those she loves keeps her from breaking, but her resolve is unraveling with each passing day…

With Aelin captured, friends and allies are scattered to different fates. Some bonds will grow even deeper, while others will be severed forever. As destinies weave together at last, all must fight if Erilea is to have any hope of salvation.

Years in the making, Sarah J. Maas's New York Times bestselling Throne of Glass series draws to an explosive conclusion as Aelin fights to save herself―and the promise of a better world.

title: Tower of Dawn (Throne of Glass, #6)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
This is a complicated one for me. It is a bit overlong and the new characters lack the substance and the ‘thing’ that made me care for the previously introduced new characters in other books from the series.

However, Chaol is and will always be one of my faves so I was happy to have a bit more intel about him and what made him to be the way he is. Yrene is also another highlight in this one.

On the other hand, I was not really invested in the whole Nesryn subplot, so because of that I was thinking about lowering it to 3.5 stars. It just felt like a complete side story that wasn’t that important to the main story... until the reveals came along.

Some of them weren’t that satisfying but the one about Maeve was top notch. I don’t know why but I gasped when I learned her backstory because I just never imagined it, to be honest.

All in all is a good book, not my favorite Throne of Glass novel out there, but it gives a lot of information regarding the Valg and all that stuff so it’s worth a read. A solid 4-star-read.

I’m not ready to finish this series, tbh 🥲
description:
Chaol Westfall and Nesryn Faliq have arrived in the shining city of Antica to forge an alliance with the Khagan of the Southern Continent, whose vast armies are Erilea's last hope. But they have also come to Antica for another purpose: to seek healing at the famed Torre Cesme for the wounds Chaol received in Rifthold.

After enduring unspeakable horrors as a child, Yrene Towers has no desire to help the young lord from Adarlan, let alone heal him. Yet she has sworn an oath to assist those in need—and will honor it. But Lord Westfall carries shadows from his own past, and Yrene soon comes to realize they could engulf them both.

In this sweeping parallel novel to the New York Times bestselling Empire of Storms, Chaol, Nesryn, and Yrene will have to draw on every scrap of their resilience if they wish to save their friends.
