But while they become entangled in the political webs of the khaganate, deep in the shadows of mighty mountains where warriors soar on legendary ruks, long-awaited answers slumber. Answers that might offer their world a chance at survival—or doom them all . . .

title: Empire of Storms (Throne of Glass, #5)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
I want to give this a million stars!!! I LOVED IT!!!

Even though at first I was afraid to be left a bit disappointed just like happened with the previous book, this was pure awesomeness from beginning to end 🤩.

I must admit that for the first half of the novel the Aelin parts were the least interesting to me because when you have Manon, Elide, Lysandra or even Dorian’s POVs you don’t really care about our almost perfect main character. Don’t get me wrong, I do like Aelin, but all of the time we’re being reminded how great she is, that she becomes just a bit too much. However by the time ‘the truth’ is revealed, I was reminded that I do appreciate her and this is HER story, above everyone else.

Nevertheless this was an amazing book, I’m really really excited to get to Kingdom of Ash, so I’ll start Tower of Dawn right now!
description:
Kingdoms will collide.

The long path to the throne has only just begun for Aelin Galathynius as war looms on the horizon. Loyalties have been broken and bought, friends have been lost and gained, and those who possess magic find themselves at odds with those who don't.

With her heart sworn to the warrior-prince by her side, and her fealty pledged to the people she is determined to save, Aelin will delve into the depths of her power to protect those she loves. But as monsters emerge from the horrors of the past, and dark forces become poised to claim her world, the only chance for salvation will lie in a desperate quest that may mark the end of everything Aelin holds dear.

In this breathtaking fifth installment of the New York Times bestselling Throne of Glass series, Aelin will have to choose what—and who—to sacrifice if she's to keep the world of Erilea from breaking apart.

title: Queen of Shadows (Throne of Glass, #4)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
This one was definitely not my favorite book in the series, and that’s probably because the previous one set the bar too high, so obviously ‘Queen of Shadows’ couldn’t match it.

I still really really liked it, I love every single character, even the new ones and the villains, and I’m excited to see what comes next. However, for some reason, I felt that the plot in this one was a little bit too transitional: stuff needed to happen in order to get to the next big thing, and that was what this book was all about: making them happen.

It still kicks some really great surprises and developments (especially in the Dorian and Manon storylines) but the whole rebel plot was maybe a little bit too convoluted for my taste... and it also has a peck of a length issue; maybe 50 pages too long, or even a 100.

Overall, a good book, but not the best ‘Throne of Glass’ novel out there
description:
Everyone Celaena Sardothien loves has been taken from her. But she’s at last returned to the empire—for vengeance, to rescue her once-glorious kingdom, and to confront the shadows of her past…

She has embraced her identity as Aelin Galathynius, Queen of Terrasen. But before she can reclaim her throne, she must fight.

She will fight for her cousin, a warrior prepared to die for her. She will fight for her friend, a young man trapped in an unspeakable prison. And she will fight for her people, enslaved to a brutal king and awaiting their lost queen’s triumphant return.

The fourth volume in the New York Times bestselling series continues Celaena’s epic journey and builds to a passionate, agonizing crescendo that might just shatter her world.

title: Heir of Fire (Throne of Glass, #3)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review: I just loved everything about this book🤩
description: Celaena has survived deadly contests and shattering heartbreak-but at an unspeakable cost. Now, she must travel to a new land to confront her darkest truth . . . a truth about her heritage that could change her life-and her future-forever. Meanwhile, brutal and monstrous forces are gathering on the horizon, intent on enslaving her world. Will Celaena find the strength to not only fight her inner demons, but to take on the evil that is about to be unleashed?

title: Crown of Midnight (Throne of Glass, #2)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
Just like the novellas book, it started kind of slow and even though I was hooked, something was missing... then *the thing* happened and it all went crazy!

Those last 150 pages are some of the most addictive I’ve ever read, so this had to be a 5 star read, but I think I’d lower it to 4.5 if I could.
description:
An assassin's loyalties are always in doubt but her heart never wavers

Assassin Celaena Sardothien won a brutal contest to become the King's Champion. But she is far from loyal to the crown. Though she hides her secret vigilantly, her deadly charade becomes difficult when she realizes she is not the only one seeking justice. No one is above questioning her allegiance—not the Crown Prince Dorian; not Chaol, the Captain of the Guard; not even her best friend, Nehemia, a foreign princess with a rebel heart.

Then, one terrible night, the secrets they have all been keeping lead to an unspeakable tragedy. As Celaena's world shatters, she will be forced to decide once and for all where her true loyalties lie ... and whom she is willing to fight for.

title: From Blood and Ash (Blood and Ash, #1)
author: Jennifer L. Armentrout
review:
OK, so I finally read the book everybody talked about a few years ago.

And I liked it. I've read many reviews since I first added 'From Blood and Ash' to my TBR, so I knew beforehand that it was repetitive, silly, and mostly a here-for-the-smut kind of book. These criticisms are true, but it's also a fun book that, at least for now, knows what it's trying to do.

It's not supposed to be deep or rich or to make sense. It's all an excuse for the romance part to exist, and in that regard, it works. There is a well-created romance with more than a few intriguing developments that make me excited for the second book.

Also, the characters are great. None of them is groundbreaking, and apart from the MCs, the other ones are too good or too evil, but the ones that matter are interesting in a SJM rip-off kind of way.

I'll keep on reading the following books. I'm intrigued, honestly.
description:
A Maiden...

Chosen from birth to usher in a new era, Poppy’s life has never been her own. The life of the Maiden is solitary. Never to be touched. Never to be looked upon. Never to be spoken to. Never to experience pleasure. Waiting for the day of her Ascension, she would rather be with the guards, fighting back the evil that took her family, than preparing to be found worthy by the gods. But the choice has never been hers.

A Duty...

The entire kingdom’s future rests on Poppy’s shoulders, something she’s not even quite sure she wants for herself. Because a Maiden has a heart. And a soul. And longing. And when Hawke, a golden-eyed guard honor bound to ensure her Ascension, enters her life, destiny and duty become tangled with desire and need. He incites her anger, makes her question everything she believes in, and tempts her with the forbidden.

A Kingdom...

Forsaken by the gods and feared by mortals, a fallen kingdom is rising once more, determined to take back what they believe is theirs through violence and vengeance. And as the shadow of those cursed draws closer, the line between what is forbidden and what is right becomes blurred. Poppy is not only on the verge of losing her heart and being found unworthy by the gods, but also her life when every blood-soaked thread that holds her world together begins to unravel.

title: Scythe (Arc of a Scythe, #1)
author: Neal Shusterman
description:
Thou shalt kill.

A world with no hunger, no disease, no war, no misery. Humanity has conquered all those things, and has even conquered death. Now scythes are the only ones who can end life—and they are commanded to do so, in order to keep the size of the population under control.

Citra and Rowan are chosen to apprentice to a scythe—a role that neither wants. These teens must master the “art” of taking life, knowing that the consequence of failure could mean losing their own.

An alternate cover edition of ISBN: 9781442472426

title: Under the Whispering Door
author: T.J. Klune
review:
Well, 'The House in The Cerulean Sea' this is not, but nor does it want to be.

'Under the Whispering Door' is a different type of story and book, even if the covers are similar, and while that's respectable for T.J. Klune, I was left a bit disappointed by the whole thing.

The book tries to be philosophical about death in many ways, and while this sometimes leads to cute moments, it also tends to bore. It is a less than 400 pages book, yet I don't think the story deserves even 300 since not much happens.

It's a typical "selfish person becomes a selfless one" narrative with allegedly some romance sprinkled on top, but I want to warn romance readers to take that with a grain of salt. This is a really slow-burn romance, and not much happens with it until the last 50 pages or so, so be aware of that.

Despite this, I can't rate it less than 3 stars. The writing is good, and any book that makes me cry deserves some praise. I won't tell what happened that made me sob, but it hit hard.

Read it, but make sure you're in the right mood for this one.
description:
Welcome to Charon's Crossing.
The tea is hot, the scones are fresh, and the dead are just passing through.

When a reaper comes to collect Wallace from his own funeral, Wallace begins to suspect he might be dead.

And when Hugo, the owner of a peculiar tea shop, promises to help him cross over, Wallace decides he’s definitely dead.

But even in death he’s not ready to abandon the life he barely lived, so when Wallace is given one week to cross over, he sets about living a lifetime in seven days.

Hilarious, haunting, and kind, Under the Whispering Door is an uplifting story about a life spent at the office and a death spent building a home.

title: Ruin and Rising (Shadow and Bone, #3)
author: Leigh Bardugo
review:
A good conclusion to the Shadow and Bone trilogy that definitely fixed some of the worst habits that plagued the previous two books, but that also had a bit of an overlong situation going on.

I must say that, all things considered, this was a good ending. It wasn't as corny or predictable as it could have been and everything had big consequences at the end. I've struggled before with YA fantasy series endings where it is all tied up a bit too neat for my taste, so it was refreshing to see that Leigh Bardugo didn't followed this route and, while still giving a happy ending, she also let the characters feel loss and grief and change.

It wasn't perfect, either. I think Bardugo's tendency to keep the characters moving and never letting them rest so they can get to the next big thing still affected the general world-building. I was really eager to know more about the Apparat (who I thought was going to have a bigger role in the ending, that was a shame) and the White Catedral, and in a matter of 50 pages that subplot was resolved in a rushed, but I must admit climactic, way. And, at the same time, around the 60% mark when we finally begin the hunt for the firebird, it draaaags for at least 3 chapters until we realize it was useless all along. It's the end of a big dramatic fantasy series, why did it felt overlong? It shouldn't have.

Some things improved, tho. Finally, 2 books and more than 600 pages later, I kinda liked Mal. Don't get me wrong, he is still one of the worst male characters in the series (he was meant to be, Nikolai and the Darkling were on another level from the start) and I never understood why Alina LOVED him that much when she had Nikolai right there asking her to marry him not once or twice, but continuously... but he wasn't annoying throughout the book, so, to me, that's a plus.

Also, I have to give props to Leigh Bardugo and her battle scenes because I think they were one of the least confusing scenes of this kind that I've ever read. The final battle, while short, was amazing in every level. Even the Darkling's death felt deserved and well timed. And Nikolai, OMG, I love that man. I think he probably is one of my favorite fictional characters ever, I'm not kidding. I need to read his Duology right now.

Anyway, at the end of the day this wasn't my favorite fantasy series from all time, BUT, I still had a lot of fun with it, so I guess that's a good thing. And now I can read 'Six of Crows' and not feel guilty about it. I'm a purist, what can I say?
description:
The Darkling rules Ravka from his shadow throne.

Now the nation's fate rests with a broken Sun Summoner, a disgraced tracker, and the shattered remnants of a once-great magical army.

Deep in an ancient network of tunnels and caverns, a weakened Alina must submit to the dubious protection of the Apparat and the zealots who worship her as a Saint. Yet her plans lie elsewhere, with the hunt for the elusive firebird and the hope that an outlaw prince still survives.

Alina will have to forge new alliances and put aside old rivalries as she and Mal race to find the last of Morozova's amplifiers. But as she begins to unravel the Darkling's secrets, she reveals a past that will forever alter her understanding of the bond they share and the power she wields. The firebird is the one thing that stands between Ravka and destruction—and claiming it could cost Alina the very future she’s fighting for.

title: Siege and Storm (Shadow and Bone, #2)
author: Leigh Bardugo
review:
A solid 4.5 star read for me!

I have to be honest, I was a bit skeptic coming into this book. The first one in this trilogy was not my favorite thing in the world: it felt like there weren't any stakes throughout the story, the characters were bland (except for the Darkling) and the world-building was flaky at best.

HOWEVER, this second book fixed many of the wrongs in the previous one and it was so good. The story was fun, the characters grew up a lot (maybe Mal not so much, but more on that in a bit), the world-building was deeper and the political intrigue + the action was amazing. I honestly would have rate this book with 5 stars, if it wasn't because of the tedious love story that Bardugo crammed in it.

It wasn't that terrible in Shadow and Bone, but probably because Mal was MIA during a big part of that book, but in here we have to deal with him from the very start, and my god... he is annoying. He's toxic, he's useless and he just ruins everything and everyone around him. I hate the person Alina becomes when he's with him, and I can't understand why she would 'love' someone like him, he's just complaining every single step of the way and literally the ONLY time he could have been useful he wasn't there. Ugh...

However, all things considered I rate my books by determining how much entertainment they brought me and even with the Mal situation I was compelled during the most part of the book (probably not that much during the first 50 pages, but after that I was in for the ride), and now I'm very excited to read the ending of the trilogy so I'll do that very soon.
description:
Hunted across the True Sea, haunted by the lives she took on the Fold, Alina must try to make a life with Mal in an unfamiliar land. She finds starting new is not easy while keeping her identity as the Sun Summoner a secret. She can’t outrun her past or her destiny for long.

The Darkling has emerged from the Shadow Fold with a terrifying new power and a dangerous plan that will test the very boundaries of the natural world. With the help of a notorious privateer, Alina returns to the country she abandoned, determined to fight the forces gathering against Ravka. But as her power grows, Alina slips deeper into the Darkling’s game of forbidden magic, and farther away from Mal. Somehow, she will have to choose between her country, her power, and the love she always thought would guide her--or risk losing everything to the oncoming storm.

title: Crooked Kingdom (Six of Crows, #2)
author: Leigh Bardugo
review:
I've never been the biggest Grishaverse fan out there.

Yes, I read the whole Shadow and Bone trilogy and this duology, but for some reason there's always something that I can really figure out what it is, that doesn't allow me to really *love* this world. However, one must give credit where credit is due.

And the truth is that this book is amazing! Not just Grishaverse amazing, but in every single way. Now I get why a lot of people are really into this series: it's twisty, the whole cast of characters is compelling, and they're really fun. The pages fly, even with the little font size, and that sensation of wanting to know what happens next is just awesome.

Also, the payback is so satisfying because you know who these characters are and the fact that Leigh Bardugo never betrays that (as opposed to what happens sometimes in Shadow and Bone) is so refreshing. We have no heroes, nor real villains, but a complicated set of people that you follow throughout the story, and while you don't really root for them, you care about what they're going through and understand their desires and motivations, and that makes for a very compelling read.

Definitely my favorite Grishaverse book so far.
description:
The #1 New York Times-bestselling sequel to Leigh Bardugo's thrilling Six of Crows.

When you can’t beat the odds, change the game.

Kaz Brekker and his crew have just pulled off a heist so daring even they didn't think they'd survive. But instead of divvying up a fat reward, they're right back to fighting for their lives. Double-crossed and badly weakened, the crew is low on resources, allies, and hope. As powerful forces from around the world descend on Ketterdam to root out the secrets of the dangerous drug known as jurda parem, old rivals and new enemies emerge to challenge Kaz's cunning and test the team's fragile loyalties. A war will be waged on the city's dark and twisting streets—a battle for revenge and redemption that will decide the fate of the Grisha world.

title: The Hero of Ages (Mistborn, #3)
author: Brandon Sanderson
review: 😭😭 4.5 stars - RTC
description:
Durant mil anys no ha canviat res: han caigut les cendres, els skaa han estat esclavitzats i el Senyor Suprem ha dominat el món. Kelsier, el «supervivent», l’únic que ha aconseguit fugir dels pous de Hathsin, juntament amb Vin, una pobra noia skaa, s’uneix a la rebel·lió. I per fi passa el que és impossible: per fi la revolució ha triomfat. Però acabar amb el Senyor Suprem és la part senzilla. El veritable desafiament consistirà a sobreviure a les conseqüències de la caiguda... sense Kelsier. title: The Well of Ascension (Mistborn, #2)
author: Brandon Sanderson
review: Not as amazing as the first one, but still good.
description:
Evil has been defeated...
The war has just begun.

They did the impossible - deposing the godlike being whose brutal rule had lasted a thousand years. Now Vin, the street urchin who has grown into the most powerful Mistborn in the land, and Elend Venture, the idealistic young nobleman who loves her, must build a healthy new society in the ashes of an empire.

They have barely begun when three separate armies attack. As the siege tightens, an ancient legend seems to offer a glimmer of hope. But even if it really exists, no one knows where to find the Well of Ascension, or what manner of power it bestows.

It may just be that killing the Lord Ruler was the easy part. Surviving the aftermath of his fall is going to be the real challenge.

title: Ninth House (Ninth House Trilogy, #1)
author: Leigh Bardugo
review: The first half was so confusing that I thought about dnf’ing, but I’m glad that I persevered because it gets amazing by the end.
description:
Galaxy “Alex” Stern is the most unlikely member of Yale’s freshman class. Raised in the Los Angeles hinterlands by a hippie mom, Alex dropped out of school early and into a world of shady drug dealer boyfriends, dead-end jobs, and much, much worse. By age twenty, in fact, she is the sole survivor of a horrific, unsolved multiple homicide. Some might say she’s thrown her life away. But at her hospital bed, Alex is offered a second chance: to attend one of the world’s most elite universities on a full ride. What’s the catch, and why her?

Still searching for answers to this herself, Alex arrives in New Haven tasked by her mysterious benefactors with monitoring the activities of Yale’s secret societies. These eight windowless “tombs” are well-known to be haunts of the future rich and powerful, from high-ranking politicos to Wall Street and Hollywood’s biggest players. But their occult activities are revealed to be more sinister and more extraordinary than any paranoid imagination might conceive.

title: The Cruel Prince (The Folk of the Air, #1)
author: Holly Black
review:
A very strong ending that almost made up for the sloooow and boring middle.

I wasn’t completely sold on this series for the most part of this book, but the last 50 pages were so good that now I’m curious. Also, I already own the three books, so why not?
description:
Of course I want to be like them. They’re beautiful as blades forged in some divine fire. They will live forever.

And Cardan is even more beautiful than the rest. I hate him more than all the others. I hate him so much that sometimes when I look at him, I can hardly breathe.

Jude was seven when her parents were murdered and she and her two sisters were stolen away to live in the treacherous High Court of Faerie. Ten years later, Jude wants nothing more than to belong there, despite her mortality. But many of the fey despise humans. Especially Prince Cardan, the youngest and wickedest son of the High King.

To win a place at the Court, she must defy him–and face the consequences.

As Jude becomes more deeply embroiled in palace intrigues and deceptions, she discovers her own capacity for trickery and bloodshed. But as betrayal threatens to drown the Courts of Faerie in violence, Jude will need to risk her life in a dangerous alliance to save her sisters, and Faerie itself.

title: The Priory of the Orange Tree (The Roots of Chaos, #1)
author: Samantha Shannon
review:
It is a bit too long, perhaps 50 less pages would have been ideal, but the amazing world building and the characters made up for almost any fault.

A solid 4.5-stars read
description:
A world divided.
A queendom without an heir.
An ancient enemy awakens.

The House of Berethnet has ruled Inys for a thousand years. Still unwed, Queen Sabran the Ninth must conceive a daughter to protect her realm from destruction—but assassins are getting closer to her door.

Ead Duryan is an outsider at court. Though she has risen to the position of lady-in-waiting, she is loyal to a hidden society of mages. Ead keeps a watchful eye on Sabran, secretly protecting her with forbidden magic.

Across the dark sea, Tané has trained all her life to be a dragonrider, but is forced to make a choice that could see her life unravel.

Meanwhile, the divided East and West refuse to parley, and forces of chaos are rising from their sleep.

An alternative cover edition for this ISBN can be found here.

title: Shadow and Bone (Shadow and Bone, #1)
author: Leigh Bardugo
review:
Uhm... I really don't know how to feel.

To be honest, I didn't cared about anything that was happening throughout the book until 2/3 of it, and that was because the characters were so very bland that I just wasn't invested in them. I don't need to like the characters in a book I'm reading, but I need to feel that I care about what they are going through, and that didn't happen until the big twist with the Darkling (and that is because he IS the best character in this whole book)

I have to admit I was a bit shocked by it, but it's frustrating to feel that this could have been so much better if the relationship between Alina and the Darkling had been treated with a little more care, it was so sudden and so rushed that when I got to that point, it was surprising, but not as much as it should have been.

Another big problem I had with this one was the lack of stakes during almost the whole book. Of course we had at the beginning the Shadow Fold situation, then the arrival of Alina to the Palace and all the shenanigans that happened in there, but it was just so basic and lack of emotion that I wasn't compelled by any of it. Did we really need a whole chapter describing how Alina was going to dress for the ball? I don't think so.

But we could have had a whole chapter about the journey that Mal and Alina had after they escaped the city (which in all fairness existed, but it felt truly rushed) and how they reconnected or a detailed account of a big lesson with Baghra, but we were kept from that and it seemed like the author was rushing their characters to get to the next big thing.

It might seem like I didn't liked it at all, but that's not true, actually. I think this world has a lot of potential (I actually believe that, in time, I'll appreciate the whole Grishaverse), the last 100 pages or so were actually great and the Darkling was an awesome character. I just wished that his awesomeness was carried over to the rest of the book.
description:
Surrounded by enemies, the once-great nation of Ravka has been torn in two by the Shadow Fold, a swath of near impenetrable darkness crawling with monsters who feast on human flesh. Now its fate may rest on the shoulders of one lonely refugee.

Alina Starkov has never been good at anything. But when her regiment is attacked on the Fold and her best friend is brutally injured, Alina reveals a dormant power that saves his life—a power that could be the key to setting her war-ravaged country free. Wrenched from everything she knows, Alina is whisked away to the royal court to be trained as a member of the Grisha, the magical elite led by the mysterious Darkling.

Yet nothing in this lavish world is what it seems. With darkness looming and an entire kingdom depending on her untamed power, Alina will have to confront the secrets of the Grisha . . . and the secrets of her heart.

Shadow and Bone is the first installment in Leigh Bardugo's Grisha Trilogy.

title: These Violent Delights (These Violent Delights, #1)
author: Chloe Gong
review:
This was an amazing 4.5 star read to me.

Even though it took me a few more days than usual to finish this book, I enjoyed it immensely. It was engaging, the characters were amazing, the twists were good and the romance, while not that prominent as I thought it would be, was complicated and interesting.

I must say I'm not so sure how the story could have a second part, I think the cliffhanger was a bit of an afterthought because the main storyline for the book was resolved by the end of it, so I was not the biggest fan of the ending... that cliffhanger for me was just for the sake of having a second book. HOWEVER, Chloe Gong really surprised me. I can't believe this is her debut because it was that amazing, I mean... I could feel Shanghai and I knew what to expect from it due to her characterization of a city. If that is not good writing, then I don't know what is... so that's why even if I'm not 100% sold on the idea of a sequel, I'm all in and I really hope to be proven wrong.
description:
The year is 1926, and Shanghai hums to the tune of debauchery.

A blood feud between two gangs runs the streets red, leaving the city helpless in the grip of chaos. At the heart of it all is eighteen-year-old Juliette Cai, a former flapper who has returned to assume her role as the proud heir of the Scarlet Gang—a network of criminals far above the law. Their only rivals in power are the White Flowers, who have fought the Scarlets for generations. And behind every move is their heir, Roma Montagov, Juliette’s first love…and first betrayal.

But when gangsters on both sides show signs of instability culminating in clawing their own throats out, the people start to whisper. Of a contagion, a madness. Of a monster in the shadows. As the deaths stack up, Juliette and Roma must set their guns—and grudges—aside and work together, for if they can’t stop this mayhem, then there will be no city left for either to rule.

Perfect for fans of The Last Magician and Descendant of the Crane, this heart-stopping debut is an imaginative Romeo and Juliet retelling set in 1920s Shanghai, with rival gangs and a monster in the depths of the Huangpu River.

title: Elantris (Elantris, #1)
author: Brandon Sanderson
review: It is a tad slow and some characters are a bit simple, but the whole Hrathen arc and the last few chapters are top notch.
description:
In 2005, Brandon Sanderson debuted with Elantris, an epic fantasy unlike any other then on the market. To celebrate its tenth anniversary, Tor is reissuing Elantris in a special edition, a fresh chance to introduce it to the myriad readers who have since become Sanderson fans.

This new edition begins with a preface by author Dan Wells, the first person to read the completed novel, and a new afterword by Sanderson explaining how he came to write the book and its place in the Cosmere, the unified universe of all his Tor novels.

Also included is an expanded version of the "Ars Arcanum" appendix, with more of the technical details of the book's magic that fans can never get enough of.

Elantris was truly a milestone both for Sanderson and for the genre of epic fantasy. It deserves this special treatment, something Tor has done only once before, with Orson Scott Card's Ender's Game. Sanderson fans old and new will be excited to discover it.

title: The Poppy War (The Poppy War, #1)
author: R.F. Kuang
review:
OMG, I loved this one.

Truth be told, I'm a skeptic about books that are major on TikTok. Despite that, I always end up reading them just for curiosity.

Going into The Poppy War, I didn't know what to expect, because I didn't even read what it was about before starting it, and it surprised me amazingly. It's a book that, even if you can feel how raw it is because of its writing, doesn't really show the extent of its crudeness until the last third. And boy, it does.

Do we have a charismatic or easy-to-root-for main character? Not at all, but we do have a complicated morally-grey young woman who is full of rage because of how her world works, and the most impressive thing about all of it is that you can understand some of her awful actions throughout the book.

It may seem like it starts like another chosen-one story or a "magic school" one, but it ends up becoming so much more.

Do check your trigger warnings before reading it, because it does have many graphic disturbing descriptions, but it's still a really good read.
description:
An epic historical military fantasy, inspired by the bloody history of China’s twentieth century and filled with treachery and magic.

When Rin aced the Keju—the Empire-wide test to find the most talented youth to learn at the Academies—it was a shock to everyone: to the test officials, who couldn’t believe a war orphan from Rooster Province could pass without cheating; to Rin’s guardians, who believed they’d finally be able to marry her off and further their criminal enterprise; and to Rin herself, who realized she was finally free of the servitude and despair that had made up her daily existence. That she got into Sinegard—the most elite military school in Nikan—was even more surprising.

But surprises aren’t always good.

Because being a dark-skinned peasant girl from the south is not an easy thing at Sinegard. Targeted from the outset by rival classmates for her color, poverty, and gender, Rin discovers she possesses a lethal, unearthly power—an aptitude for the nearly-mythical art of shamanism. Exploring the depths of her gift with the help of a seemingly insane teacher and psychoactive substances, Rin learns that gods long thought dead are very much alive—and that mastering control over those powers could mean more than just surviving school.

For while the Nikara Empire is at peace, the Federation of Mugen still lurks across a narrow sea. The militarily advanced Federation occupied Nikan for decades after the First Poppy War, and only barely lost the continent in the Second. And while most of the people are complacent to go about their lives, a few are aware that a Third Poppy War is just a spark away . . .

Rin’s shamanic powers may be the only way to save her people. But as she finds out more about the god that has chosen her, the vengeful Phoenix, she fears that winning the war may cost her humanity . . . and that it may already be too late.

title: The Final Empire (Mistborn, #1)
author: Brandon Sanderson
review:
When I started this book, I was nervous because the hype was huge, and the 'Cosmere' it's simply enormous. It demands many hours and many books to take advantage of it, so I was intimidated to be disappointed.

Boy, I was wrong.

Like I said in my mini post-finished review, this is easily my favorite book of the year, and I can't really pinpoint a reason why since there are many reasons.

For starters, I found a new favorite fictional character in Kelsier. Also, maybe I wasn't paying attention to the foreshadowing, but there were many twists I never saw coming, especially the one almost at the end that I'm not going to spoil, but that impressed me like few books have done before.

Also, the fact that the author really took his time to make you care about these characters was amazing. I'm terrible with names in these types of books, but from the start until the end, I was able to understand who was talking and what role every person had in the story.

I've been a fantasy reader for a while, but my comfort zone is in the YA fantasy/romance novels. I don't care. I really like how the romance leads those stories, and I don't get why many people look down upon them, but that made me nervous to start this one.

'The Final Empire' was my first adult fantasy series (besides City of Brass) with a hard magic system but it definitely won't be my last. I appreciate how Sanderson's writing felt pretty accessible throughout the whole book and it feels like the correct decision to start with this trilogy and this universe before moving to maybe more complicated stories and series.

However, I must admit that I still suck when it comes to battle scenes, and this magic system didn't really make it any easier for me. But I think that's mostly on me. I still loved it.
description:
What if the whole world were a dead, blasted wasteland?

Mistborn
For a thousand years the ash fell and no flowers bloomed. For a thousand years the Skaa slaved in misery and lived in fear. For a thousand years the Lord Ruler, the "Sliver of Infinity," reigned with absolute power and ultimate terror, divinely invincible. Then, when hope was so long lost that not even its memory remained, a terribly scarred, heart-broken half-Skaa rediscovered it in the depths of the Lord Ruler's most hellish prison. Kelsier "snapped" and found in himself the powers of a Mistborn. A brilliant thief and natural leader, he turned his talents to the ultimate caper, with the Lord Ruler himself as the mark.

Kelsier recruited the underworld's elite, the smartest and most trustworthy allomancers, each of whom shares one of his many powers, and all of whom relish a high-stakes challenge. Then Kelsier reveals his ultimate dream, not just the greatest heist in history, but the downfall of the divine despot.

But even with the best criminal crew ever assembled, Kel's plan looks more like the ultimate long shot, until luck brings a ragged girl named Vin into his life. Like him, she's a half-Skaa orphan, but she's lived a much harsher life. Vin has learned to expect betrayal from everyone she meets. She will have to learn trust if Kel is to help her master powers of which she never dreamed.

Brandon Sanderson, fantasy's newest master tale-spinner and author of the acclaimed debut Elantris, dares to turn a genre on its head by asking a simple question: What if the prophesied hero failed to defeat the Dark Lord? The answer will be found in the Mistborn Trilogy, a saga of surprises that begins with the book in your hands. Fantasy will never be the same again.

title: La vida invisible de Addie LaRue
author: V.E. Schwab
review:
Okay, so I wasn't blown away by this one.

Truth be told: I don't get the appeal. For me it was a typical YA romance with an interesting fantasy twist but that was repetitive to the extreme. Every time there was a scene in the past I knew that Addie was going to be someplace historic and that Luc would appear so they could have a chat about his powers and her previous wishes, have some witty banter, then he would disappear. Every. Single. Time.

And while the chapters in the present were a bit more interesting, there was no real build-up between Henry and Addie relationship: they just got to know each other, discovered that they were both cursed so they fell in love because of it.

They were interesting enough by themselves, but their relationship, at least for me, was more of a desperate thing, and I don't think this was what the author was going for in this case.

All in all, I didn't hate it, nor did I really like it... it was just meh! Although the writing was amazing, that much I have to admit, and the ending was fitting. Not shocking or precisely unpredictable, but it tied everything as best as this irregular story could be ended.
description:
Una vida que nadie recuerda.
Una historia que nunca olvidarás.

Francia, 1714. En un momento de desesperación, una joven hace un pacto faustiano para conseguir una vida infinita. ¿Cuál es el precio que deberá pagar para vivir eternamente? El olvido. Todas y cada una de las personas que conoce la terminarán olvidando.

Así es cómo comienza la extraordinaria vida de Addie LaRue; una vida que atraviesa siglos y continentes, una vida que atraviesa la historia y el arte, en la que ella intenta comprender hasta dónde será capaz de llegar con tal de dejar su marca en el mundo.

Sin embargo, todo cambia cuando, después de 300 años, Addie conoce a un hombre en una librería. Pero hay algo más… él es la única persona que recuerda su nombre.

title: The Lightning Thief (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #1)
author: Rick Riordan
review:
This was a fun, quick and easy 4 star read. Even though I knew some of the things that happened in here because I watched the movie back when it came out, the book still surprised me in a big way, and now I understand why everyone just kind of hates them.

I won't say I was gripped to the pages, because I don't think it's that kind of a book, but it's still a good one and I'm all in for a feel-good series scattered here and there throughout some other other fantasy-heavy or contemporary books that I usually read.
description:
Alternate cover for this ISBN can be found here

Percy Jackson is a good kid, but he can't seem to focus on his schoolwork or control his temper. And lately, being away at boarding school is only getting worse - Percy could have sworn his pre-algebra teacher turned into a monster and tried to kill him. When Percy's mom finds out, she knows it's time that he knew the truth about where he came from, and that he go to the one place he'll be safe. She sends Percy to Camp Half Blood, a summer camp for demigods (on Long Island), where he learns that the father he never knew is Poseidon, God of the Sea. Soon a mystery unfolds and together with his friends—one a satyr and the other the demigod daughter of Athena - Percy sets out on a quest across the United States to reach the gates of the Underworld (located in a recording studio in Hollywood) and prevent a catastrophic war between the gods.

title: Six of Crows (Six of Crows, #1)
author: Leigh Bardugo
review:
I finished this a few hours ago, and I knew that I needed to take a moment to really take in the whole book so I could give an appropriate review, and here it is.

It is a really good book, it's exciting, the characters are amazing (Nina being my personal favorite) and the heist is really fun. I think the last 200 pages are impossible to not read in a single sitting because everything is happening at the same time and there are big events in almost every single chapter, that it's hard not to fall into a 'just one more chapter' situation. So far, so good.

I actually thought about rating it with 5 stars, but I just can't look away from the confusion that the first 100 pages brought to the whole experience. There were so many characters introduced at once (even though a lot of them weren't important at ALL during the rest of the book) and the plot was just confusing and kind of all over the place that even though I read the entire Shadow and Bone trilogy, I was still confused, so I can't see how someone who just started the Grishaverse with this one can understand what was going on.

After the initial chapters and then, when everything started to fall into place I could see why this story is beloved and hyped throughout the book community, but I do think that the hype is probably a bit too high. It's good, I liked it, and of course I'll read the second one, but calling it one of my favorite books EVER... I don't think so.
description:
Alternate cover of ISBN 9781627792127

Ketterdam: a bustling hub of international trade where anything can be had for the right price—and no one knows that better than criminal prodigy Kaz Brekker. Kaz is offered a chance at a deadly heist that could make him rich beyond his wildest dreams. But he can’t pull it off alone...

A convict with a thirst for revenge

A sharpshooter who can’t walk away from a wager

A runaway with a privileged past

A spy known as the Wraith

A Heartrender using her magic to survive the slums

A thief with a gift for unlikely escapes

Six dangerous outcasts. One impossible heist. Kaz’s crew is the only thing that might stand between the world and destruction—if they don’t kill each other first.

title: The House in the Cerulean Sea (Cerulean Chronicles, #1)
author: T.J. Klune
review:
Words can't describe how much I loved this book!

I must admit, at first I was a little lost when Linus arrived at the island and gets to know the kids for the first time because, since I'm not really a fantasy reader (I'll fix that this year), I don't really know how the whole "world-building" part of a fantasy usually works, so it took me a few pages to really *feel* the book.

However, once I overcame this little part and started to get to really know the kids and Arthur and Zoe, and even Linus when he started to come out of his shell, the story just clicked really deep in me. It has a really cute and important message and I seriously think that every tween, teen or simply any person should read this.

I laughed, I cried and I definitely didn't wanted it to end. And I guess this last part means that what T.J. Klune wrote is really special. Also, yay for representation!

I'm sure this book will be one of my faves not just of the year... but of my all time favorites.
description:
Linus Baker is a by-the-book case worker in the Department in Charge of Magical Youth. He's tasked with determining whether six dangerous magical children are likely to bring about the end of the world.

Arthur Parnassus is the master of the orphanage. He would do anything to keep the children safe, even if it means the world will burn. And his secrets will come to light.

The House in the Cerulean Sea is an enchanting love story, masterfully told, about the profound experience of discovering an unlikely family in an unexpected place—and realizing that family is yours.

title: A Court of Thorns and Roses (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #1)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
I knew SJM wouldn’t let me down.

At the beginning, I was nervous with this one because I was 150 pages in and I wasn’t sure where we were going. The characters were a bit annoying, the plot wasn’t that exciting and I just thought “how can this story deserve so many books?”

Well, it fooled me. When Feyre and Tamlin started to care for each other and the love story kicked in, I was in for the ride. I believe that I read the second half of the book in just 2 days because I needed to know what was happening. The revelations about the curse were so obvious once they were laid out that I was shocked that it never crossed my mind. That was awesome.

Then, when the story took Feyre Under the Mountain I was delighted to discover that this wasn’t another TOG situation where we were just told about what happened. Not anymore. The tasks were amazing and so exciting, and I was gasping when the final one arrived.

In short, while not perfect, I can see why this is such a beloved series and I WILL be reading the next books.
description:
The tantalising start to a seductive fantasy series from global #1 bestselling author Sarah J. Maas.

Feyre is a huntress. And when she sees a deer in the forest being pursued by a wolf, she kills the predator and takes its prey to feed herself and her family.

But the wolf was not what it seemed, and Feyre cannot predict the high price she will have to pay for its death...

Dragged away from her family for the murder of a faerie, Feyre discovers that her captor, his face obscured by a jewelled mask, is hiding even more than his piercing green eyes suggest.

As Feyre's feelings for Tamlin turn from hostility to passion, she learns that the faerie lands are a far more dangerous place than she realized. And Feyre must fight to break an ancient curse, or she will lose him forever.

title: Leviathan Wakes
author: James S.A. Corey
review:
I mean... wow!

Coming into my first science fiction novel, I wasn't sure what to expect, and it probably wasn't this, but I have absolutely no complaints.

I don't know why this book is nowhere to be found on Booktok or Bookstagram, because I think it checks every single thing people that use those platforms look for in a book, except probably romance. Which it has, but it's not the main conflict in here at any point. But boy, it deserves a lot more recognition.

For a little while now I've been searching for an adventure book more in the style of Indiana Jones and such where the characters were unraveling mysteries and being trapped with more questions than answers throughout the story. And while this book is located in space, and it has NO similarities to what I was looking for, it definitely cured the thirst for it. It IS adventurous and action-filled, it has an amazing mystery (that is mostly resolved by the end) full of organic twists and turns, and it's just so much fun.

Yes, it does have a bit of an overlong situation and a bit of a been-there-done-that thing going on, where a pattern was starting to repeat every 100 pages or so, but these constant challenges for the characters really invigorated the plot and raised its stakes for the most part.

I do have some hopes for the following books, and is related to the thing I just mentioned. The author needs to let the characters breathe for a second, so we can get to know them a bit more, especially our SC which are awesome, but they feel trapped in an over saturated plot. I just said it was kind of an overlong book, but I think if we had those moments (even if the book turned out to be a bit longer) it would have had more gravitas as a whole.

I'm just picking hairs right now, this is an awesome book, and it deserves 5 amazing stars.
description:
Humanity has colonized the solar system—Mars, the Moon, the Asteroid Belt and beyond—but the stars are still out of our reach.

Jim Holden is XO of an ice miner making runs from the rings of Saturn to the mining stations of the Belt. When he and his crew stumble upon a derelict ship, the Scopuli, they find themselves in possession of a secret they never wanted. A secret that someone is willing to kill for—and kill on a scale unfathomable to Jim and his crew. War is brewing in the system unless he can find out who left the ship and why.

Detective Miller is looking for a girl. One girl in a system of billions, but her parents have money and money talks. When the trail leads him to the Scopuli and rebel sympathizer Holden, he realizes that this girl may be the key to everything.

Holden and Miller must thread the needle between the Earth government, the Outer Planet revolutionaries, and secretive corporations—and the odds are against them. But out in the Belt, the rules are different, and one small ship can change the fate of the universe.

title: Know My Name
author: Chanel Miller
description:
She was known to the world as Emily Doe when she stunned millions with a letter. Brock Turner had been sentenced to just six months in county jail after he was found sexually assaulting her on Stanford’s campus. Her victim impact statement was posted on BuzzFeed, where it instantly went viral–viewed by eleven million people within four days, it was translated globally and read on the floor of Congress; it inspired changes in California law and the recall of the judge in the case. Thousands wrote to say that she had given them the courage to share their own experiences of assault for the first time.

Now she reclaims her identity to tell her story of trauma, transcendence, and the power of words. It was the perfect case, in many ways–there were eyewitnesses, Turner ran away, physical evidence was immediately secured. But her struggles with isolation and shame during the aftermath and the trial reveal the oppression victims face in even the best-case scenarios. Her story illuminates a culture biased to protect perpetrators, indicts a criminal justice system designed to fail the most vulnerable, and, ultimately, shines with the courage required to move through suffering and live a full and beautiful life.

Know My Name will forever transform the way we think about sexual assault, challenging our beliefs about what is acceptable and speaking truth to the tumultuous reality of healing. It also introduces readers to an extraordinary writer, one whose words have already changed our world. Entwining pain, resilience, and humor, this memoir will stand as a modern classic.

title: Mexican Gothic
author: Silvia Moreno-Garcia
review: Gross, stupid and boring. I hated everything about it, except the first quarter, where a sense of something interesting could be glimpsed, but that ultimately failed horribly.
description:
After receiving a frantic letter from her newly-wed cousin begging for someone to save her from a mysterious doom, Noemí Taboada heads to High Place, a distant house in the Mexican countryside. She’s not sure what she will find—her cousin’s husband, a handsome Englishman, is a stranger, and Noemí knows little about the region.

Noemí is also an unlikely rescuer: She’s a glamorous debutante, and her chic gowns and perfect red lipstick are more suited for cocktail parties than amateur sleuthing. But she’s also tough and smart, with an indomitable will, and she is not afraid: Not of her cousin’s new husband, who is both menacing and alluring; not of his father, the ancient patriarch who seems to be fascinated by Noemí; and not even of the house itself, which begins to invade Noemi’s dreams with visions of blood and doom.

Her only ally in this inhospitable abode is the family’s youngest son. Shy and gentle, he seems to want to help Noemí, but might also be hiding dark knowledge of his family’s past. For there are many secrets behind the walls of High Place. The family’s once colossal wealth and faded mining empire kept them from prying eyes, but as Noemí digs deeper she unearths stories of violence and madness.

And Noemí, mesmerized by the terrifying yet seductive world of High Place, may soon find it impossible to ever leave this enigmatic house behind.

title: The Midnight Library (The Midnight World, #1)
author: Matt Haig
review:
The ending is really good and the story is mostly cute and heartbreaking, but I think it faces some pacing and predictability issues that I can’t ignore.

I don’t think is the best book of 2020, but I do get the appeal of why a lot of people think it is, I just wished that the fantasy/sci fi element of it was further explored.

This will be a great movie, tho, that much I can tell.
description:
Between life and death there is a library.

When Nora Seed finds herself in the Midnight Library, she has a chance to make things right. Up until now, her life has been full of misery and regret. She feels she has let everyone down, including herself. But things are about to change.

The books in the Midnight Library enable Nora to live as if she had done things differently. With the help of an old friend, she can now undo every one of her regrets as she tries to work out her perfect life. But things aren't always what she imagined they'd be, and soon her choices place the library and herself in extreme danger.

Before time runs out, she must answer the ultimate question: what is the best way to live?

title: Una tierra prometida
author: Barack Obama
review:
200 pages too long, probably, but it still is a very interesting recount of the first half of Obama's administration.

I would have liked to have a bit more intel on how his family adapted to the public life, tho. We do get some information regarding Michelle Obama and their daughters, but I just wished it had more, especially because the first third of the book is lot more autobiographical and then that aspect suddenly stopped.
I get this is a book about his presidency, not his family, so I'll pass that.

However, the long descriptions about some of the regulations and laws he tried to pass tended to go on and on and on, resulting sometimes on me skim reading through some passages because I just wanted to get to the next thing. Also, there are some really looooong chapters, which I'm not really a fan of.

So, all in all, the first 300 pages were a 5 star read for me, then the middle chapters around a 3.5, and finally the last hundred pages it ticked up to a 4, which is how I think I really feel about this behemoth of a book: a solid 4 stars read.
description:
En este esperado y emocionante primer volumen de sus memorias presidenciales, Barack Obama nos cuenta la historia de su inaudita trayectoria: cómo un joven en busca de su identidad se convirtió en líder del mundo occidental, al tiempo que describe el sumo detalle tanto su formación política como los momentos cruciales del primer mandato de su histórica presidencia, una época de grandes conmociones y de profundos cambios.

Obama nos acompaña en un viaje increíble que abarca desde sus más tempranas aspiraciones en el mundo de la política hasta la emotiva noche del 4 de noviembre de 2008, cuando fue elegido presidente número 44 de Estados Unidos y se convirtió así en el primer afroamericano en ocupar el cargo más alto de la nación.

Con sus reflexiones en torno a la presidencia, Obama no solo nos ofrece un análisis único y profundo del alcance y los límites del poder, sino que también nos brinca una visión singular del funcionamiento de la política estadounidense y la diplomacia internacional. Nos hace partícipes de sus pensamientos mientras compone su gabinete, lidia con una crisis financiera global, sopesa a Vladimir Putin, vence obstáculos aparentemente insuperables para lograr la aprobación de la reforma sanitaria, se enfrenta a generales sobre la estrategia de Estados Unidos en Afganistán, aborda la reforma de Wall Street, responde al devastador derrame de petróleo de Deepwater Horizon, y autoriza la Operación Lanza de Neptuno, que culmina con la muerte de Osama bin Laden.

Una tierra prometida es un libro único, personal e introspectivo que narra la apuesta de un hombre con la historia, la fe de un trabajador comunitario puesta a prueba ante el mundo. Obama expone el difícil equilibrio entre hacer campaña como afroamericano - cargando con la expectativas de una generación ilusionada por ideales como << esperanza>> y <> - y enfrentarse al desafío moral del tener que tomar decisiones de gran trascendencia.

Aquí no habla con franqueza de las fuerzas que se le opusieron tanto en su país como en el extranjero, revela cómo la vida en la Casa Blanca afectó a su esposa y a sus hijas, y no teme confesarnos sus inseguridades ni decepciones, sin dejar de lado su convicción de que, dentro del gran experimento americano, el progreso siembre es posible.

Con una prosa exquisita, este impactante libro captura y contagia la poderosa convicción de Barack Obama en torno a la idea de democracia: no es un don del cielo, sino un espacio basado en la empatía y la comprensión mutua, que construimos entre todos a diario.

title: The City of Brass (The Daevabad Trilogy, #1)
author: S.A. Chakraborty
review:
This one took me more time that I thought it would take, but it wasn't particularly for the book. The world just decided to not give me almost any time to read, so it took me 9 days to finish it.

I must say I really liked it, even though at times the world-building is a little bit tricky and because the book has the tendency to keep information until later, sometimes you don't really know *exactly* what the characters are talking about and I didn't liked that at all. It was probably to build suspense or to create some sort of mystery, but it tended to became tedious.

Around 200 pages in, it all sort of... clicks. But you really need to take the time to repeat to yourself some of the whole tribes situation, because there are 6 of them, and a lot of unknown words that are quite complicated to connect at first, and it can get overwhelming.

In short, it is a great book and a good start for this series that I'm really eager to continue!
description:
Nahri has never believed in magic. Certainly, she has power; on the streets of 18th century Cairo, she’s a con woman of unsurpassed talent. But she knows better than anyone that the trade she uses to get by—palm readings, zars, healings—are all tricks, sleights of hand, learned skills; a means to the delightful end of swindling Ottoman nobles.

But when Nahri accidentally summons an equally sly, darkly mysterious djinn warrior to her side during one of her cons, she’s forced to accept that the magical world she thought only existed in childhood stories is real. For the warrior tells her a new tale: across hot, windswept sands teeming with creatures of fire, and rivers where the mythical marid sleep; past ruins of once-magnificent human metropolises, and mountains where the circling hawks are not what they seem, lies Daevabad, the legendary city of brass, a city to which Nahri is irrevocably bound.

In that city, behind gilded brass walls laced with enchantments, behind the six gates of the six djinn tribes, old resentments are simmering. And when Nahri decides to enter this world, she learns that true power is fierce and brutal. That magic cannot shield her from the dangerous web of court politics. That even the cleverest of schemes can have deadly consequences.

After all, there is a reason they say be careful what you wish for...

title: House of Earth and Blood (Crescent City, #1)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
This was simply amazing!

Even though the first 150 pages are a bit too expository, once you get the hang of the world and the characters it all comes together nicely and the real fun begins.

I really can’t explain how much I loved this world and these characters. And this comes from someone who, at first, wasn’t really sure if that was going to happen because there was so much information thrown at once and the characters weren’t… you know… likable enough that made me care about what was happening. But OMG how much that changed.

I can already say that Hunt is my favorite Sarah J Maas character from today until the day I die. He was a gem. Gladly, in time, Bryce and Ruhn became so much more interesting that what I first thought, so I liked them too, but no one reached Hunt’s awesomeness.

I’m so excited for the second book. Even though I think this could have been a standalone (there’s no real cliffhanger, and it could have worked out without the epilogue) I trust in Maas that the story needs to be a trilogy… or a long series since she loves that.
description:
Bryce Quinlan had the perfect life-working hard all day and partying all night-until a demon murdered her closest friends, leaving her bereft, wounded, and alone. When the accused is behind bars but the crimes start up again, Bryce finds herself at the heart of the investigation. She'll do whatever it takes to avenge their deaths.

Hunt Athalar is a notorious Fallen angel, now enslaved to the Archangels he once attempted to overthrow. His brutal skills and incredible strength have been set to one purpose-to assassinate his boss's enemies, no questions asked. But with a demon wreaking havoc in the city, he's offered an irresistible deal: help Bryce find the murderer, and his freedom will be within reach.

As Bryce and Hunt dig deep into Crescent City's underbelly, they discover a dark power that threatens everything and everyone they hold dear, and they find, in each other, a blazing passion-one that could set them both free, if they'd only let it.

With unforgettable characters, sizzling romance, and page-turning suspense, this richly inventive new fantasy series delves into the heartache of loss, the price of freedom-and the power of love.

title: Ready Player One (Ready Player One, #1)
author: Ernest Cline
description:
A world at stake.
A quest for the ultimate prize.
Are you ready?
It’s the year 2044, and the real world is an ugly place.
Like most of humanity, Wade Watts escapes his grim surroundings by spending his waking hours jacked into the OASIS, a sprawling virtual utopia that lets you be anything you want to be, a place where you can live and play and fall in love on any of ten thousand planets.

And like most of humanity, Wade dreams of being the one to discover the ultimate lottery ticket that lies concealed within this virtual world. For somewhere inside this giant networked playground, OASIS creator James Halliday has hidden a series of fiendish puzzles that will yield massive fortune—and remarkable power—to whoever can unlock them.

For years, millions have struggled fruitlessly to attain this prize, knowing only that Halliday’s riddles are based in the pop culture he loved—that of the late twentieth century. And for years, millions have found in this quest another means of escape, retreating into happy, obsessive study of Halliday’s icons. Like many of his contemporaries, Wade is as comfortable debating the finer points of John Hughes’s oeuvre, playing Pac-Man, or reciting Devo lyrics as he is scrounging power to run his OASIS rig.

And then Wade stumbles upon the first puzzle.

Suddenly the whole world is watching, and thousands of competitors join the hunt—among them certain powerful players who are willing to commit very real murder to beat Wade to this prize. Now the only way for Wade to survive and preserve everything he knows is to win. But to do so, he may have to leave behind his oh-so-perfect virtual existence and face up to life—and love—in the real world he’s always been so desperate to escape.

title: The Meaning of Mariah Carey
author: Mariah Carey
review:
I may be really biased when it comes to this book and Mariah in general because I'm a big fan of hers, so I'm just going to say that if you like her... read this. It really gives you a lot of intel about her and her life (which I'm gonna admit is much more tragic than her diva persona may suggest).

Definitely the best chapters are the first one where she goes around her childhood and gets to share some really private moments when racism, sadness, hate, fear and loneliness flooded her life, and the third one when she goes full disclosure about the whole Glitter debacle. These are gut-wrenching and really elevate the narrative (and Mariah not just as an artist, but as a person) to previously unrecognized territory.

I wasn't in love with every single part of the book, though. I felt like this narrative sometimes got lost with all the name-dropping (especially in the second part) that happens when she talks about her writing process and her collaborations with some artists or producers, and maybe those pages could have been filled with more information about the "why" of more of her songs. These little pieces of information (I especially loved when she talked about "The Roof") were some of the best parts of the book, and I was craving for some more. However this is not a big complaint, and I was hooked to the pages all the way through.

All things considered, and she makes it clear several times, this book is for the fans, so if you're part of the Lambily, go on and read it. It is worth it!

If you're not, it still is a heartbreaking and inspiring story of how one of the biggest artists of all time came to be.
description:
It took me a lifetime to have the courage and the clarity to write my memoir. I want to tell the story of the moments - the ups and downs, the triumphs and traumas, the debacles and the dreams, that contributed to the person I am today. Though there have been countless stories about me throughout my career and very public personal life, it’s been impossible to communicate the complexities and depths of my experience in any single magazine article or a ten-minute television interview. And even then, my words were filtered through someone else’s lens, largely satisfying someone else’s assignment to define me.

This book is composed of my memories, my mishaps, my struggles, my survival and my songs. Unfiltered. I went deep into my childhood and gave the scared little girl inside of me a big voice. I let the abandoned and ambitious adolescent have her say, and the betrayed and triumphant woman I became tell her side.

Writing this memoir was incredibly hard, humbling and healing. My sincere hope is that you are moved to a new understanding, not only about me, but also about the resilience of the human spirit.

Love,
Mariah

title: Throne of Glass (Throne of Glass, #1)
author: Sarah J. Maas
review:
I LOVED THISSSSS!!

Even though the Tests were a bit of a letdown altogether and the 'twist' that happened with Cain was extremely predictable, I just need to know what happens next.

I'm hooked!
description:
In a land without magic, where the king rules with an iron hand, an assassin is summoned to the castle. She comes not to kill the king, but to win her freedom. If she defeats twenty-three killers, thieves, and warriors in a competition, she is released from prison to serve as the king's champion. Her name is Celaena Sardothien.

The Crown Prince will provoke her. The Captain of the Guard will protect her. But something evil dwells in the castle of glass—and it's there to kill. When her competitors start dying one by one, Celaena's fight for freedom becomes a fight for survival, and a desperate quest to root out the evil before it destroys her world.

title: El dolor de la cigüeña
author: Daniela Richer
description: Las campanadas rompieron el silencio de la madrugada para anunciar que estaban frente a una auténtica emergencia; una pareja hostil ha invadido las instalaciones del único orfanato de una remota localidad española durante la época franquista, en donde el personal asegura que irrumpieron con la intención de robarse a un niño. Tras alertar a las autoridades locales, un comandante y un joven agente se disponen a esclarecer el motivo de la transgresión, descubriendo que el incidente está conectado con un secreto que ha permanecido sepultado durante años. Cuando una nueva ola de secuestros asalta el lugar, son ellos quienes siguen la pista que promete ponerle fin a la investigación, la cual para su sorpresa, apenas está por comenzar.

title: Volverás a Alaska
author: Kristin Hannah
review:
I don't even know why I didn't loved this book, but I'm noticing how this type of sub-genre is not really for me. I tried earlier this year with 'Where the Crawdads Sing' and I got the same feel that I can't connect with this whole "different and often overlooked girl who is stranded in a nobody's land scenario who is forced to grow alone with everything against her" narrative.

Adding to the fact that the book is around 100 pages too long, the characters weren't really that interesting to justify them. Of course Leni was going to beat every obstacle on her way, and even though Cora is a flawed and much more developed character than her, I never understood why suddenly in the last couple of chapters everyone in Alaska was so fond of her. She had a rough life and she deserved better, but in any part of the book she was shown really developing a connection with another person but her family so it doesn't ring true. The rest of the characters were as flat as they may be and I must admit I never bothered to know how the whole Mad Earl family was even composed; they were just names dropped in the middle of the narrative with no real personalities or purpose.

But not everything is bad, of course. I'm still rating it with 3 stars because the story was -at times- interesting, the romance bits were sweet and the author really took the time to paint Alaska and its wildlife. I also believe the first half of the book is much better than the second one: probably because we were seeing it all through the eyes of Leni as a kid instead of as an adult, something that I've noticed is common in these type of books.

All in all, it was a pleasant read that I don't regret... but I'm not sure I would recommend either. Probably I'll think differently once I read 'The Nightingale' but I don't think that will be very soon.
description:
De la autora del best seller internacional El Ruiseñor, una épica historia de amor, pérdida y supervivencia que celebra la resistencia del espíritu humano y la inquebrantable fuerza de las mujeres.

Alaska, 1974. Indómita. Impredecible.

Y para una familia en crisis, la prueba definitiva.

Ernt Allbright vuelve de la guerra de Vietnam convertido en un hombre distinto. Incapaz de mantener un trabajo, toma una decisión impulsiva: toda su familia comenzará una nueva vida en la salvaje Alaska, la última frontera.

Con apenas 13 años, su hija Leni ansía encontrar su lugar en el mundo, mientras que su mujer, Cora, estaría dispuesta a cualquier cosa por el hombre al que ama, aunque eso signifique seguirle en su aventura hacia lo desconocido.

En una inhóspita y remota esquina del país, los Allbright encontraran una pequeña comunidad de hombres aguerridos y mujeres aún más fuertes en la que labrarse un nuevo futuro. Allí, Leni tendrá que madurar muy deprisa, enfrentándose al desafío de una naturaleza desmesurada y cruel, a lo que oculta su propia familia y a la tormentosa relación de sus padres. Pero cuando el invierno llegue y el frío y la oscuridad lo invadan todo, madre e hija descubrirán que, en un entorno hostil, nadie puede salvarte más que tú mismo.

title: One Last Stop
author: Casey McQuiston
review:
Another 4 star read courtesy of Casey McQuiston.

This year I haven't been reading so many contemporary rom-coms, and instead I've been into a lot of fantasy, so this was a nice change of pace, and while it wasn't my favorite read ever, it was cute, fun and mostly light-hearted.

The characters were, just like in her previous book, amazing. Every single one was unique, well developed and actually brought something to the table. I'm not just talking about the diversity (which was appreciated) but regarding the semi-heist August & Co. had to get through in order to help Jane. Everyone had an important role and for me that was really satisfying.

The sci-fi element in here really worked, too. It brings some logistics issues, but this is a rom-com, so we can forgive some physics being thrown out the window. The important thing about it was how it was affecting our characters and I think McQuiston did an amazing job in that department.

Not as amazing? Our mystery element in the book. I know no one who picks up this book was expecting the whole 'let's figure out who Jane is' to be really treated like a mystery, or even the Uncle Auggie situation, but, I believe that if you bring this little-almost-insignificant-until-the-end-speck-of-mystery to the table, commit to it. Everything regarding Jane's past and her connection with August's uncle was held back from the reader until it was convenient for the plot to be remembered. Every time the story needed to move forward, there was Jane who casually just recalled something from her time so August could place another piece of the puzzle together, and it just, for me (a reader who is really fond of the mystery genre) felt cheap. I mean, if August was supposed to be this Nancy Drew kind of girl because of how her mom brought her up, then at least give her the chance to show her detective skills. Unfortunately, maybe because a mystery writer McQuiston is not and she purposefully decided to do it this way, or maybe the mystery was a bit of a headache for her, she went for the most hated device on any mystery book.

Anyway, at the end of the day, I did liked this book. I think McQuiston is a very interesting queer voice who always puts LGBTQ+ stories up and front, and that's something to appreciate. This seems to be like an experimental book (and a great one) and I can't wait to see how she continues to grow as a writer.
description:
For cynical twenty-three-year-old August, moving to New York City is supposed to prove her right: that things like magic and cinematic love stories don’t exist, and the only smart way to go through life is alone. She can’t imagine how waiting tables at a 24-hour pancake diner and moving in with too many weird roommates could possibly change that. And there’s certainly no chance of her subway commute being anything more than a daily trudge through boredom and electrical failures.

But then, there’s this gorgeous girl on the train.

Jane. Dazzling, charming, mysterious, impossible Jane. Jane with her rough edges and swoopy hair and soft smile, showing up in a leather jacket to save August’s day when she needed it most. August’s subway crush becomes the best part of her day, but pretty soon, she discovers there’s one big problem: Jane doesn’t just look like an old school punk rocker. She’s literally displaced in time from the 1970s, and August is going to have to use everything she tried to leave in her own past to help her. Maybe it’s time to start believing in some things, after all.

Casey McQuiston’s One Last Stop is a magical, sexy, big-hearted romance where the impossible becomes possible as August does everything in her power to save the girl lost in time.

title: One for the Money (Stephanie Plum, #1)
author: Janet Evanovich
description: With over 235,000 five-star ratings, this “snappily written, fast-paced, and witty” series starter (USA Today) introduces feisty out-of-work bounty hunter Stephanie Plum, who takes a job as an apprehension agent and winds up getting assigned to track down and arrest her former flame, an ex-cop charged with murder.

title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind – The #1 New York Times Bestseller Exploring Evolution and Ancient Socieities
author: Yuval Noah Harari
review:
3.5 stars actually.

Even though I was enthralled during the entire book, the whole thing was like a rollercoaster in the sense of having pronounced ups and downs. Some chapters were really good and offered a lot of interesting facts about humans (especially during the first half) but in others I was almost skim-reading through them because they were so long and not that engaging.

I don't regret reading it at all, and probably I'll read the Homo Deus one, but I think I'll take a few months break between them.
description:
From a renowned historian comes a groundbreaking narrative of humanity’s creation and evolution—a #1 international bestseller—that explores the ways in which biology and history have defined us and enhanced our understanding of what it means to be “human.”

One hundred thousand years ago, at least six different species of humans inhabited Earth. Yet today there is only one—homo sapiens. What happened to the others? And what may happen to us?

Most books about the history of humanity pursue either a historical or a biological approach, but Dr. Yuval Noah Harari breaks the mold with this highly original book that begins about 70,000 years ago with the appearance of modern cognition. From examining the role evolving humans have played in the global ecosystem to charting the rise of empires, Sapiens integrates history and science to reconsider accepted narratives, connect past developments with contemporary concerns, and examine specific events within the context of larger ideas.

Dr. Harari also compels us to look ahead, because over the last few decades humans have begun to bend laws of natural selection that have governed life for the past four billion years. We are acquiring the ability to design not only the world around us, but also ourselves. Where is this leading us, and what do we want to become?

Featuring 27 photographs, 6 maps, and 25 illustrations/diagrams, this provocative and insightful work is sure to spark debate and is essential reading for aficionados of Jared Diamond, James Gleick, Matt Ridley, Robert Wright, and Sharon Moalem.

title: In a Holidaze
author: Christina Lauren
review:
3 stars for me.

I was never really THAT invested throughout the book, but it definitely clicked a little bit in me.

For a moment I thought it would be a bit more sci-fi than it ended up being and I actually think that the book suffers because of this. I know it was a silly romance from the start, and those parts were cute, but I think it could have been so much better if the authors embraced the time-loop even more into the story.

Anyway, from the get-go you know if you're into these type of books or not, but even if you are... I don't think this one is one of the best out there.
description:
SOON TO BE A NETFLIX FILM STARRING MADDIE ZIEGLER, ROB LOWE, GRAHAM PHILLIPS, AND ELIAS KACAVAS
THE INSTANT NEW YORK TIMES BESTSELLER

“Pure, irresistible magic from start to finish.” —Emily Henry, #1 New York Times bestselling author

One Christmas wish, two brothers, and a lifetime of hope are on the line for hapless Maelyn Jones in this quintessential holiday romantic comedy by Christina Lauren, the New York Times bestselling authors of The Paradise Problem.

It's the most wonderful time of the year...but not for Maelyn Jones. She's living with her parents, hates her going-nowhere job, and has just made a romantic error of epic proportions. But perhaps worst of all, this is the last Christmas she will spend at her favorite place in the world: the snowy Utah cabin where her family has spent the holidays every year since she was born. Mae throws out a plea to the universe: Please. Show me what will make me happy.

Everything goes black, but then she gasps awake on an airplane bound for Utah, where the same holiday begins all over again. With one hilarious disaster after another sending her back to the plane, Mae must break free of the time loop—and finally get her true love under the mistletoe.

title: Anxious People
author: Fredrik Backman
review:
I was really torn between giving this book 3 or 4 stars.

It started out very strong, then kind of fizzled in the middle but then I got to the last 100 pages and it just won me and I decided to give it 4.
